text:
In the Court of Appeal of Alberta

Citation: R. v. Keegstra, 1994 ABCA 293

Date:
19940907

Docket:
13537

Registry:
Calgary

Between:

Her Majesty The Queen

Respondent

- and -

James Keegstra

Appellant

The Court:

The Honourable Mr. Justice Harradence

The Honourable Madam Justice Hetherington

The Honourable Mr. Justice Foisy

Reasons for Judgment of The Honourable Mr.
Justice Harradence Reasons for Judgment of The Honourable Madam Justice
Hetherington Concurring

Reasons for Judgment of The Honourable Mr.
Justice Foisy Dissenting

APPEAL FROM THE JUDGMENT OF THE HONOURABLE
MR. JUSTICE LUTZ OF THE COURT OF QUEEN'S BENCH OF ALBERTA DATED JULY 10, 1992

COUNSEL:

Jack Watson Q.C., for the Respondent

Douglas H. Christie, for the Appellant

REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT OF

THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE HARRADENCE

FACTS

[
1
]

The accused was a high school teacher in Eckville
until he was dismissed in 1982 on the grounds that he gave anti-Semitic
lectures while teaching social studies. An appeal of this dismissal was heard
by a Court of Queen's Bench judge sitting as a Board of Reference pursuant to
the
School Act,
R.S.A. 1980, c. s-3: see
Keegstra
v.
Board of
Education of the County of Lacombe # 14

(1983), 45 A.R. 348
. That appeal
was dismissed.

[
2
]

Mr. Keegstra was subsequently charged in 1984
with unlawfully promoting hatred against an identifiable group under s.
281.2(2) [now s. 319(2)] of the
Criminal Code
.
Prior to his first trial,
Mr. Keegstra mounted two
Charter
attacks in Court of Queen's Bench
against the constitutionality of s. 319(2) for violating the s. 2(b) freedom of
expression, and a violation of the s. 11 (d) presumption of innocence caused by
the reverse onus contained in the truth defence in s. 319(3)(a). This
application was dismissed and the accused was subsequently tried and convicted
by a jury. The sentence was a $5000.00 fine.

[
3
]

The accused then raised the same
Charter
issues
on appeal. This appeal, reported at
R.
v.
Keegstra
(1988)
1988 ABCA 234 (CanLII)
, 87 A.R.
177, was successful as both the charging section and truth defence were
declared unconstitutional. Upon a Crown appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada,
reported as
R.
v.
Keegstra
(1990),
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 61 C.C.C. (3d) 1, that
decision was reversed. The Supreme Court remitted the case back to this Court
for determination of issues which were not originally dealt with because of the
constitutional rulings. In supplementary reasons reported at (1991),
1991 ABCA 97 (CanLII)
, 114 A.R.
288, this court quashed the accused's conviction and ordered a new trial on the
basis that the trial judge erred in not allowing the accused to challenge potential
jurors for cause on account of the significant pretrial publicity.

[
4
]

The jury began hearing evidence in the accused's
retrial on March 9, 1992. This
trial lasted four months. Twenty witnesses were called, 17 of whom were former
students of Mr. Keegstra. Only two of these students had their memories
sufficiently refreshed from their class notes to give independent evidence. The
evidence of the other 15 witnesses was admitted via their notes under the past
recollection recorded rule. Of the three remaining witnesses, one was the
teacher who replaced Mr. Keegstra, one was the superintendent of the school
district in which Mr. Keegstra taught, and the final witness was an expert in
Judaism.

[
5
]

The accused was again found guilty and he
received a sentence of a $3000.00 fine.

[
6
]

The accused appealed this conviction on a myriad
of issues. The majority of these grounds were dismissed from the bench and the
Crown was asked to respond to only four issues. The Appellant framed these
issues as follows:

1.     That the provisions of Section
319(2) and (3) are void for vagueness as defined in more recent cases of the
Supreme Court of Canada, contrary to section 7 and should be struck down by

Section 52
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
.

2.     Did the trial judge err in his
definition of public interest and public benefit assuming these words are not
so vague as to be constitutionally invalid?

3.     The trial judge erred in unduly
restricting the cross examination and set bad legal rulings in the way of an
unrepresented accused who was properly cross-examining in the instances of
Maddox, Roth, and Ramstead from evidence in a previous trial.

4.     The trial judge erred in not
giving the jury (a) copy of the trial transcript of Robert David's evidence
when requested and (b) a copy of
sections 319(2)
and
(3)
of the
Criminal
Code

on request.

CONSTITUTIONAL ISSUES

[
7
]

Appellant's counsel submits that the defence
subsections under
s. 319(3)
are void for vagueness and therefore violate the accused's

Charter
rights. These provisions are said to contain terms which are
vague, subjective and constitute a standardless sweep. As such, he submits that
the defences in
s. 319(3)
do not meet the requirements of certainty by
supplying adequate grounds for legal debate. In addition, the defences are
argued to not provide the requirements of fair notice to citizens and
limitation on law enforcement discretion, nor are the terms capable of being
given a constant and settled meaning. In this regard,
R.
v.
Nova Scotia
Pharmaceutical Society
(1992),
1992 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, 93 D.L.R. (4th) 36 (S.C.C.), and
R.
v.
Morales

(1992),
1992 CanLII 53 (SCC)
, 77 C.C.C. (3d) 91 (S.C.C.) are relied upon.

[
8
]

The Crown's main response to this contention is
that it is incomprehensible for a defendant to attack the words in a defence as
overly broad. The Appellant counters arguing that the subsections in
s. 319(3)

define the
s. 319(2)
offence by exclusion. Indeed, for this argument to benefit
the accused,
s. 319(3)
must be considered to define the offence. For how can it
be of any assistance to the defendant to have a defence struck down under
s.
52(1)
of the
Constitution Act,
1982 as unconstitutionally vague?

[
9
]

Stated another way, the defences must be
considered as essential elements of the offence. In this context, the essential
elements are defined as those factors which the Crown must either prove or
negate beyond a reasonable doubt. This is contrasted with defences where the
accused bears at least an evidential burden of production, or where the facts
must suggest a defence before any onus is cast upon the Crown.

[
10
]

The answer to whether or not the provisions in
s. 319(3) delineate the offence of wilfully promoting hatred is found in an
interpretation of ss. 319(2) and (3). Subsections 319(2) and (3) state:

(2) Every one who, by communicating
statements, other than in private conversation, wilfully promotes hatred
against an identifiable group is guilty of

(a) an
indictable offence and is liable to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two
years; or

(b) an
offence punishable on summary conviction.

(3) No person shall be convicted of an
offence under subsection (2)

(a) if he establishes that the
statements communicated were true;

(b) if, in good faith, he
expressed or attempted to establish by argument an opinion upon a religious
subject;

(c) if the statements were
relevant to any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the
public benefit, and if on reasonable grounds he believed them to be true; or

(d) if, in good faith, he intended
to point out, for the purpose of removal, matters producing or tending to
produce feelings of hatred towards an identifiable group in Canada.

[
11
]

Guidance in the interpretation of a penal
statute is provided in
R.
v.
Paul
(1982),
1982 CanLII 179 (SCC)
, 42 N.R. 1 (S.C.C.) at
41 where Lamer, J. (as he then was) quoted the early case of
Attorney
General
v.
Lockwood
(1842), 9 M. & W. 378;
152 E.R. 160
, as
typical of the legal pronouncements on the interpretation of penal statutes,
and in particular, where an exceptional construction may be given:

The rule of law, I take it, upon the
construction of all statutes, and therefore applicable to the construction of
this, is, whether they be penal or remedial, to construe them according to the
plain, literal, and grammatical meaning of the words in which they are
expressed, unless that construction leads to a plain and clear contradiction of
the apparent purpose of the act, or to some palpable and evident absurdity.

[
12
]

The principle of strict construction where any
reasonable ambiguity in a penal statute must be resolved for the benefit of an
accused also applies:
R.
v.
Paul
,
supra
at 13. Here, the
appellant's argument is only tenable if there is a reasonable ambiguity which
indicates that
s. 319(3)
contains essential elements of the offence of wilfully
promoting hatred.

[
13
]

With these principles in mind, I am of opinion
that it was not Parliament's intention that s, 319(3) define or delineate the
offence of wilfully promoting hatred; nor that those provisions constitute an
element which the Crown bears the onus of negating beyond a reasonable doubt in
every case. This intention is evidenced in several ways.

[
14
]

First, and most importantly, the opening words
of the subsection are that "No person shall be convicted of an offence
under subsection (2)". This wording indicates that a completely defined
offence is constituted in ss. (2). Indeed, all of the constituent elements of a
criminal offence are contained in
s. 319(2)
(i.e. the
actus
reus
is the promotion of hatred against
an identifiable group by communicating statements other than in private
conversation, and the
mens rea
is the wilful promotion of hatred in
those prescribed circumstances).

[
15
]

Second, it is also significant that the offence
elements in ss. (2) are separate from the circumstances in ss. (3) which allow
an accused to escape conviction. The House of Lords in
R.
v.
Hunt
,

[1987] 1 All E.R. 1
, referred to the significance of this in deciding where the
burden of proof lay. Lord Griffiths stated (at 10):

It presents particularly difficult
problems of construction when what might be regarded as a matter of defence
appears in a clause creating the offence rather than in some subsequent proviso
from which it may more readily be inferred that it was intended to provide for
a separate defence which a defendant must set up and prove if he wishes to
avail himself of it.

I do not wish to be taken as saying that the
provisions in s. 319(3) (b)-(d) must be proven by a defendant. Rather, just
that the separation of the factors presented in
s. 319(3)
from the elements in

s. 319(2)
indicates Parliament's intent to allow for a set of defences apart
from the essential elements of the offence.

[
16
]

Third, as Kerans, J.A. pointed out in
R.

v.
Keegstra
(1988),
1988 ABCA 234 (CanLII)
, 87 A.R. 177 (C.A.) at 184, a traditional approach of
the criminal law is to distinguish elements of an offence essential to guilt
from "defences" by the fact that defences do not necessarily arise in
every case. This is a helpful approach here as it would be unusual that
Parliament intended for the Crown to negate all of the elements in
s. 319(3)
in
every case.

[
17
]

Fourth, the reverse onus in the truth defence in

ss. 319(3)
(a) is an important consideration. Although reverse onuses do not
appear in subsections (b), (c), or (d), the proximity of those subsections with
the truth defence illustrates Parliament's intention that they are not to be
considered as elements of the offence.

[
18
]

Finally, these subsections can be properly
characterized as defences. Although the line between what is a defence and what
is an element of an offence can be blurred at times, particularly when a
defence is simply casting doubt on the existence of either the
mens rea

or
actus reus
of an offence, or where the purported defences may appear
in the section that creates the offence, these subsections are capable of being
interpreted as what some commentators have called 'true" or
"affirmative" defences. That is, defences which exonerate an accused
despite the admitted existence of all of the essential elements of the crime
(see R. Mahoney,
The Presumption of Innocence: a New Era"
(1988),
67 Can. Bar Rev. 1.). These
"true" defences have generally been recognized in the category of
justification whereas defences which question the existence of an essential
element are sometimes coined as excuses. Dickson, J. in
R.
v.
Perka

(1984),
1984 CanLII 23 (SCC)
, 42 C.R. (3d) 113 at 128 (S.C.C.) C.J.C. defined these defences as
follows:

Criminaltheory recognizes a distinction
between "justifications" and "excuses". A
"justification" challenges the wrongfulness of an action which
technically constitutes a crime…

In contrast, an "excuse"
concedes the wrongfulness of an action but asserts that the circumstances under
which it was done are such that it ought not be attributed to the actor. The
perpetrator who is incapable, owing to a disease of the mind, of appreciating
the nature and consequences of his acts, the person who labours under a mistake
of fact, the drunkard, the sleepwalker: these are all actors of whose criminal
actions we disapprove intensely, but whom, in appropriate circumstances, our
law will not punish.

[
19
]

In general, the defences found in ss. 319(3)
(b)-(d) are capable of falling into the justification category. Although
Dickson, C.J.C. indicates in
R.
v.
Keegstra
(1990),
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 61 C.C.C.
(3d) 1 (S.C.C.) that it would be rare for a person who fell under one of these
defences to have the requisite intent necessary for a conviction under
s.
319(2)
, it is possible that there may be situations where an accused intended
to wilfully promote hatred yet did so under one of the precepts of the defences
under
s. 319(3)
. As such, these defences are capable of exonerating an accused
despite the existence of all of the elements which technically constitute a
crime. Since these provisions are capable of acting as justifications for what
would otherwise subject an accused to criminal sanction, Parliament's intention
to restrict the definitional elements of the actual offence to
ss. 319(2)
is
again evidenced.

[
20
]

This interpretation is strengthened by analogies
to other areas of the
Criminal Code
. For instance, the self defence provision
in s. 34 of the
Code
justifies the assault or killing of another in prescribed
circumstances. It has never been suggested, nor could such a suggestion be
accepted, that the absence of self-defence defines the offence of assault in s.
265. Although the Crown must negative self-defence to obtain a conviction if
the facts indicate, or the defence raises the possibility of this defence
existing, there is no onus on the Crown to prove an absence of self-defence in
every prosecution. As such, self-defence operates as a justification for what
would otherwise be the crime of assault. Similarly, although the Crown may be
required to negative the existence of one of the
s. 319(3)
(b)-(d) defences if
the evidence indicates such a defence is open to the accused, or if the defence
puts such a defence into issue, it does not mean that the Crown is required to
dispel the defences in every case. In this regard, I do not think the proximity
of
s. 319(2)
to
s. 319(3)
has any significance.

[
21
]

Mr. Justice Dickson's majority comments in
R.

v.
Keegstra (No. 1)
(1990),
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 61 C.C.C. (3d) 1 (S.C.C.). support this
interpretation (at 60-61):

The factors mentioned above suggest that
s. 319(2) does not unduly restrict the s. 2(b) guarantee. The terms of the
offence, as I have defined them, rather indicate that s. 319(2) possesses
definitional limits which act as safeguards to ensure that it will capture only
expressive activity which is openly hostile to Parliament's objective, and will
thus attack only the harm at which the prohibition is targeted. The specific
defences provided are further glosses on the purview of the offence…

A careful reading of the s. 319(3)
defences shows them to take in examples of expressive activity that generally
would not fall within the "wilful promotion of hatred" as I have
defined the phrase. Thus the three defences which include elements of good
faith or honest belief -- namely,
s. 319(3)
(b), (c) and (d) -- would seem to
operate to negate directly the
mens rea
in the offence, for only rarely
will one who intends to promote hatred be acting in good faith or upon honest
belief. These defences are hence intended to aid in making the scope of the
wilful promotion of hatred more explicit; individuals engaging in the type of
expression described are thus given a strong signal that their activity will
not be swept into the ambit of the offence. The result is that what danger
exists that
s. 319(2)
is overbroad or unduly vague, or will be perceived as
such, is significantly reduced. To the extent that
s. 319(3)
provides
justification for the accused who would otherwise fall within the parameters of
the offence of wilfully promoting hatred, it reflects a commitment to the idea
that an individuals's freedom of expression will not be curtailed in borderline
cases. The line between the rough and tumble of public debate and brutal,
negative and damaging attacks upon identifiable groups is hence adjusted in
order to give some leeway to freedom of expression.

[
22
]

Although Dickson, C.J.C. referring to the
defences as "glosses on the purview of the offence" could infer
definitional limits for the offence, when the above passage is read as a whole,
it is clear that is not what he intended. For instance, he refers to
s. 319(2)

itself providing the definitional limits of the offence. The defences may place
a "gloss" on the reach of the offence, but this does not mean that
the offence is defined by requiring the Crown to exclude the presence of
circumstances set out in
s. 319(3)
in every case. As well,
s. 319(3)
is
repeatedly said to contain defences. Obviously the court was of opinion that
those provisions were not elements which must be negated by the Crown in every
case.

[
23
]

Finally, Dickson, C.J.C. refers to
s. 319(3)

providing justification for an accused's actions when they would otherwise fall
within the parameters of wilfully promoting hatred. The defences do not define
or delineate even though they limit the purview of the offence by what Mr.
Justice Dickson calls giving leeway to the freedom of expression. Overall, it
is clear that the Supreme Court did not consider the offence of wilfully
promoting hatred to be defined by the defences set out in
s. 319(3)
.

Vagueness

[
24
]

Assuming that the defences were linked to the
offence in such a way that they defined the charging section by exclusion, an
analysis if those terms are impermissibly vague is required. The only viable
argument here is the potential vagueness of the term "public
interest" as it appears in
s. 319(3)
(c). Other allegations that terms such
as "race," "religious subject," or "ethnic
origin" are devoid of merit and will not be addressed.

[
25
]

As a preliminary matter, it is clear that the
constitutional doctrine of vagueness does apply to defences in the
Criminal
Code
.
Gonthier, J. made this clear in
R.
v.
Nova Scotia
Pharmaceutical Society
,
supra,
at 59, where he stated that the vagueness standard
applies to all enactments:

Finally, I also wish to point out that
the standard I have outlined applies to all enactments, irrespective of whether
they are civil, criminal, administrative or other. The citizen is entitled to
have the state abide by constitutional standards of precision whenever it
enacts legal dispositions.

Similarly, Lamer, C.J.C. in
R.
v.
Morales
,

supra,
stated at 101:

If the doctrine of vagueness aims to
ensure that all dispositions are framed in terms which permit meaningful legal
debate, then all dispositions are subject to this doctrine regardless of their
form.

These statements indicate that the doctrine of
vagueness applies to defence provisions in the
Criminal Code
.

[
26
]

The next step is to determine if "public
interest" is an impermissibly vague term. In
Morales
.
Lamer, C.J.C.
held that "public interest" as a criterion for pretrial detention in
s. 515(10)(b) of the
Code
does violate the doctrine of vagueness:

In my view, these authorities do not
establish any "workable meaning" for the term "public interest".
On the contrary, these authorities demonstrate the open-ended nature of the
term … In my view, these authorities demonstrate that the term "public
interest" has not been given a constant or settled meaning by the courts.
The term provides no guidance for legal debate. The term authorizes a standardless
sweep, as the court can order imprisonment whenever it sees fit. According to
Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society at p. 313, such unfettered discretion
violates the doctrine of vagueness…

As currently defined by the courts, the
term "public interest" is incapable of framing the legal debate in
any meaningful manner or structuring discretion in any way. Nor would it be
possible in my view to give the term "public interest" a constant and
settled meaning. The term gives the courts unrestricted latitude to define any
circumstances as sufficient to justify pretrial detention. The term creates no
criteria to define these circumstances. No amount of judicial interpretation of
the term "public interest" would be capable of rendering it a
provision which gives any guidance for legal debate.

[
27
]

The necessary question then is whether the court
in
Morales
intended to pronounce that "public interest" was an
impermissibly vague term in all circumstances. In my opinion, the court's
analysis was restricted to the appearance of the term in s. 515(10)(b). The
cases Lamer, C.J.C. cites as illustrating the court's inability to define
"public interest" were all decisions dealing with pre-trial
detention. Despite some comments in
Morales
that could indicate that the
court was of the opinion that "public interest" was incapable of
being given a "constant or settled" meaning in more general terms,
all of these comments are connected to defining the term as it appears in s.
515(10)(b).

[
28
]

The recent decision of
R.
v.
Farinacci
et al.
(9 November 1993) Ontario

C10791, C13886, C11372 (Ont. C.A.) notes the key distinguishing factor in
Morales
(at 23):

.. a substantial component of the notion
of public interest, indeed its largest component in the criminal law context,
was carved out of the possible meaning of "public interest" by the
fact that
s. 515
of the
Criminal Code
contemplated the denial of bail "for
the protection and safety of the public
or
in the public interest".
The contrast between public safety and public interest left insufficient
intelligible content to the term "public interest' to satisfy the
constitutional requirement of statutory precision.

Both the court in
Farinacci
and the
British Columbia Court of Appeal in
R.
v.
Branco
(8 November 1993) Vancouver 2265/CA015818 distinguished
Morales
on the basis that Lamer,
J. restricted his conclusions to s. 515(10)(b). I agree with those decisions
that
Morales
does not stand for the principle that "public
interest" is vague in all circumstances.

[
29
]

The Supreme Court has found the term
"public interest' to be vague in another circumstance. Madam Justice McLachlin,
writing for the majority in
R.
v.
Zundel
(1992),
1992 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, 140 N.R. 1
(S.C.C.), held that the phrase "injury or mischief to a public interest,"
as it appears in the
s. 181

Criminal Code

prohibition against spreading
false news, created an undefined offence with a virtually unlimited reach. She
stated at 38:

It is difficult to see how a broad,
undefined phrase such as "public interest" can on its face constitute
a restrained, appropriately limited measure which impairs the right infringed
to the minimum degree consistent with securing legislation's objectives.

This case gives some indication of whether
"public interest" as it appears in
s. 319(3)
(c) is an impermissibly
vague term, but I do not read the case as setting down any principle that this
term is vague in all instances in which it appears in the
Criminal Code
.
McLachlin,
J.'s comments may be restricted to the
s. 181
.

[
30
]

In defining a term in the context of vagueness,
Lamer, C.J.C. commented in
Morales
,
supra,
at 101:

A provision does not violate the doctrine
of vagueness simply because it is subject to interpretation. To require
precision would be to create an impossible constitutional standard.

And Gonthier, J. in
Nova
Scotia
Pharmaceutical Society
,
supra,
at 59:

What becomes more problematic is not so
much general terms conferring broad discretion, but terms failing to give
direction as to how to exercise this discretion, so that this exercise may be
controlled. Once more, an impermissibly vague law will not provide a sufficient
basis for legal debate; it will not give a sufficient indication as to how
decisions must be reached, such as factors to be considered or determinative
elements. In giving unfettered discretion, it will deprive the judiciary of
means of controlling the exercise of this discretion.

[
31
]

Cory and lacobbuci, JJ. in the dissent in
Zundel
,
held that courts can and should define terms and words used in the
Criminal
Code
.
They cite several examples where this has occurred, with notable
examples being the Supreme Court interpreting "undue exploitation of
sex" in
R.
v.
Butler and McCord
,
1992 CanLII 124 (SCC)
, [1992] 1 S.C.R. 452, and
interpreting "other fraudulent means" in
R.
v.
Plan, Hudson
and Hartnett
,
1978 CanLII 9 (SCC)
, [1978] 2 S.C.R. 1175. In referring to the numerous times
"public interest" appears in legislation, they gave the following
method of which should be followed by the courts in defining the term (at 83):

The term does not and cannot have a
uniform meaning in each statute. It must be interpreted in light of the
legislative history of the particular provision in which it appears and the
legislative and social context in which it is used.

A "public interest" likely to
be harmed as a result of contravention of s. 181 is the public interest in a
free and democratic society that is subject to the rule of law. A free society
is one built upon reasoned debate in which all its members are entitled to
participate. Section 181, including its reference to "public interest",
should, as this court has emphasized, be interpreted in light of Charter
values.

[
32
]

The majority in
Zundel
held that the
cases which were said to establish that statutes must be interpreted in
accordance with
Charter
values did not support that proposition. Rather,
Mclachlin, J. held at 39-40:

These authorities confirm the following
basic propositions: that the common law should develop in accordance with the
values of the Charter (Salituro, supra, at p. 675), and that where a
legislative provision, on a reasonable interpretation of its history and on the
plain reading of its text, is subject to two equally persuasive
interpretations, the court should adopt that interpretation which accords with
the Charter and the values to which it gives expression (Hills and Slaight,
supra).

[
33
]

Zundel

establishes that in defining what a "subject of public interest"
means in the context of
s. 319(3)
(c), and in determining whether this term is
unconstitutionally vague, the legislative history for the provision is
important. The historical impetus for the enactment of
s. 319
of the
Criminal
Code

was the 1966 report of the Special Committee on Hate Propaganda in Canada. Dickson, C.J.C. recognized the
effect of this report in
Keegstra
,
supra,
at 20:

… the recurrent theme running throughout
the report is the need to prevent the dissemination of hate propaganda without
unduly infringing the freedom of expression, a theme which led the committee to
recommend a number of amendments to the
Criminal Code
.

[
34
]

The question then is whether there are
sufficient factors or determinative elements to provide a basis for legal
debate for s. 319(3)(c) in light of the historical and legislative history of
the section, and on a plain reading of its text.

[
35
]

Obviously the s. 319(3) (c) defence is intended
to prevent undue restriction on the freedom of expression while still allowing
for the criminalization of hate propaganda. Dickson, C.J.C. in
Keegstra
,

supra,
at 61, commented on the effect of the defences saying that they
were "a committment to the idea that an individual's freedom of expression
will not be curtailed in borderline cases".

[
36
]

This committment is balanced against the harms
sought to be avoided by prohibiting the wilful promotion of hatred. The two
main harms identified by Dickson, C.J.C. are the harm to a target groups' sense
of human dignity and belonging to the community, and the harm to society in
general where hate propaganda causes serious discord between cultural groups.

[
37
]

The nature of the defences as justifications, as
mentioned above, may allow an accused to escape conviction even where it has
been found that the offence of s. 319(2) has been committed. "Public
interest' must therefore be defined on the basis of where the value to society
in giving leeway to the freedom of expression exceeds the public interest in
preventing the harm that results from the dissemination of hatred. But at which
point is the freedom of expression unduly curtailed by the offence of wilfully
promoting hatred?

[
38
]

In my opinion, there is little or any guidance
in the historical development of
s. 319
which grounds a definition of what
subject matter is relevant to the "public interest" in the terms of
the defences. As Mclachlin, J. noted in
Zundel
.

supra,
the term
"public interest" is broad and undefined. This is true in the present
case as well. There is no discernible method for distinguishing when the value
to society inherent in the freedom of expression exceeds the value to society
in prohibiting the dissemination of hate.

[
39
]

A plain reading of the text also fails to
provide a workable definition of what a "subject of public interest"
is. Subsection 319(3)(c) states that in addition to the statements needing to
be relevant to a subject matter of public interest, the discussion must be for
the "public benefit." This wording suggests that something may not be
for the public benefit yet may still be "relevant to any subject of public
interest." For instance, sensational matters may be a "subject matter
of public interest" though a discussion of that subject matter may not be
for the public benefit. The subsection as a whole indicates that there is no
internal guidance as to the meaning of "public interest."

[
40
]

In sum, the phrase "relevant to any subject
of public interest" is vague. Neither the historical development, nor the
wording of the section give any basis for how decisions are to be reached or
give a sufficient basis for legal debate. The dividing line between what is a
subject matter relevant to the public interest in terms of the freedom of
expression and the harms sought to be avoided by
s. 319(2)
is indiscernible.

Effect of Vagueness

[
41
]

The next inquiry is what effect declaring the
section void for vagueness would have in this case. First, the severability of
the section must be determined. On this point, I agree with the Crown that ss.
319(3) (c) is imminently severable. Lamer, C.J.C. in
Morales
,
supra,
at
110, states the test for severability as follows:

R. v. Wholesale Travel Group Inc. (1991),

1991 CanLII 39 (SCC)
, 67 C.C.C. (3d) 193 at p. 229, 84 D.L.R. (4th) 161, [1991] 3 S.C.R. 154, held
that a severable portion of a statutory provision can be struck down without
having to strike down the entire provision, provided that severance would not
defeat a "unitary scheme" envisaged by Parliament. Severance does not
usurp Parliament's role, but rather is the approach which best fulfils the
terms of
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
, which provides that a law
which is inconsistent with the Constitution is of no force and effect 'to the
extent of the inconsistency". Severance is also least intrusive to the
over-all statutory scheme.

[
42
]

The severability of the subsection is reflected
in the constitutional significance attributable to an impermissibly vague
defence. The constitutional significance of a void provision is summarized by Gonthier,
J. in
Nova Scotia

Pharmaceutical Society
,
supra,
at 48:

1. Vagueness can be raised under s. 7 of
the Charter, since it is a principle of fundamental justice that laws may not
be too vague. It can also be raised under s. 1 of the Charter in limine, on the
basis that an enactment is so vague as not to satisfy the requirement that a
limitation on Charter rights be "prescribed by law". Furthermore,
vagueness is also relevant to the "minimal impairment" stage of the
Oakes test…

[
43
]

It must first be noted that courts are reluctant
to find a provision so vague as to not qualify as a "limit prescribed by
law" under s. 1 of the
Charter;
rather, the courts will prefer to
consider the scope of the provision under the "minimal impairment"
test:
R.
v.
Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society
,
supra,
at
48. In
Osborne
v.
Canada
(Treasury Board)
(1991),
1991 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, 82 D.L.R.
(4th) 321 (S.C.C.) at 339, Sopinka J. referred to the requirements which must
be met in order to strike a law down as for not being "prescribed by
law":

A law may be so uncertain as to be
incapable of being interpreted so as to constitute any restraint on
governmental power. The uncertainty may arise either from the generality of the
discretion conferred on the donee of the power or from the use of language that
is so obscure as to be incapable of interpretation with any degree of precision
using the ordinary tools. In these circumstances, there is no "limit
prescribed by law" and no s. 1 analysis is necessary as the threshold
requirement for its application is not met.

[
44
]

In my opinion, whether a limit is
"prescribed by law" is not the question when determining the
constitutional significance of a vague defence. The vagueness of s. 319(3) (c)
does not confer unrestrained power on the government.
Section 319(2)
is the primary
restraint on governmental power in the scheme of prohibiting hate propaganda.

[
45
]

I also do not consider the proper approach in
this circumstance to fall under s. 7 of the
Charter
which provides:

7. Everyone has the right to life,
liberty and security of the person and the right not to be deprived thereof
except in accordance with the principles of fundamental justice.

A provision aimed at allowing an accused to
escape conviction cannot be considered to restrict his liberty. As the court in

Branco
,
supra,
noted in regard to s. 679(3)(c) of the
Code:

the appellant's liberty interests can
only be enhanced by s. 679(3)(c).

Such an observation applies to s. 319(3).
Logically, an overly broad defence provision could only enhance an accused's
liberty interest by allowing latitude in argument as to what conduct would
allow an accused to escape conviction.

[
46
]

Consequently, the only basis on which the
provisions in s. 319(3) can be argued to be vague is in relation to s. 1 of the

Charter
under the "minimal impairment' portion of the
Oakes

test. In this regard it is clear that s. 319(3) played a role in Dickson,
C.J.C.'s determination that the offence section in
s. 319(2)
was not overly
broad. The question then is what effect a determination that a provision in s.
319(3) was vague would have on the s. 1 analysis in the Supreme Court decision
in
Keegstra.

supra.
In my opinion, it would have little effect.
This is clear from Dickson, C.J.C.'s remarks regarding the truth defence (at
62):

The way in which I have defined the s.
319(2) offence, in the context of the objective sought by society and the value
of the prohibited expression, gives me some doubt as to whether the Charter
mandates that truthful statements communicated
with an intention to promote
hatred
need be excepted from criminal condemnation.

[
47
]

This statement indicates the willingness of the
Supreme Court to uphold the constitutionality of the offence even if one could
be charged when disseminating truthful statements. The value inherent in the
freedom of expression when connected to truthful statements is self-evident. If
the Supreme Court could attach constitutional validity to an offence of
promoting hatred even though the statements communicated were true, then surely
by inference the offence section would withstand any determination that the
other defences in s. 319(3) were void for vagueness. Hence, even if s. 319(3)
(c) was unconstitutionally vague, severing the section from the defined offence
in
s. 319(2)
would not have the effect of making the purview of the offence so
wide as to violate the minimal impairment stage of the
Oakes
test.

Trial Judge's Definition of Public Interest

[
48
]

Aside from arguments that the s. 319(3) is
vague, counsel for the Appellant advanced the further ground of appeal that the
trial judge erred in his definition of "public interest" and
"public benefit" as they appear in s. 319(3)(c). Having determined
that the subsection is indeed vague, it is unnecessary to determine whether the
trial judge erred in defining the "public interest" as it appears in the
defence. Indeed, the trial judge cannot be faulted for the definition he gave
to the provision in light of the difficulty in discerning what is
"relevant to any subject of public interest."

[

In arguing that this was an error, the Appellant
relies on s. 10(1) of the
Canada
Evidence Act,
R.S., E-10 which
provides:

On any trial a witness may be
cross-examined as to previous statements made by him in writing, or reduced to
writing, relative to the subject-matter of the case, without the writing being
shown to him, but, if it is intended to contradict the witness by the writing,
his attention must, before the contradictory proof can be given, be called to
those parts of the writing that are to be used for the purpose of so
contradicting him, and the judge, at any time during the trial, may require the
production of the writing for his inspection, and thereupon make such use of it
for the purposes of the trial as he thinks fit.

[
53
]

Section 10(1) has received interpretation in a
number of cases. In
Cormier
v.
The Queen

(1973), 25 C.R.N.S. 94
(Que. C.A.)
, the proper
interpretation of the effect of s. 10(1) of the
Canada
Evidence Act
on the cross-examination
of a witness on a written statement was stated as follows at 98:

As I see it, the only limitation to this
type of cross-examination is that contained in s. 10(1), that is to say that,
"if it is intended to contradict the witness by the writing, his attention
must, before such contradictory proof can be given, be called to those parts of
the writing that are used for the purpose of so contradicting him". That
is a long way from saying that counsel must first satisfy the Judge that there
are, in fact, contradictions.

[
54
]

This view was also taken by the Ontario Court of
Appeal in
R.
v.
Valley
(1986),
1986 CanLII 4609 (ON CA)
, 26 C.C.C. (3d) 207, [leave to
appeal to S.C.C. ref'd], and in
R.
v.
Savion and Mizrahi
(1980).
52 C.C.C. (2d) 277.

[
55
]

Similarly, this court commented on the effect of
s. 10 in
R.
v.
Whitford
(1990),
1990 ABCA 131 (CanLII)
, 105 A.R. 274, where Kerans, J.A.
stated (at 275):

Section 10, on the other hand, permits a
party opposite to cross-examine a witness about previous statements. There is
no requirement in that section that the judge make an advance ruling about
inconsistency.

Kerans, J.A. also referred to the restriction of
cross-examination:

Cross-examining counsel is, as all the
cases agree, to be given a wide ambit. Cross-examination should be permitted
except where it would be abusive.

[
56
]

These cases, and a plain reading of s. 10(1)
itself, make it clear that there is no need to establish a contradiction
between present testimony and a previous statement reduced to writing before an
accused is entitled to cross-examine on it. There is no authority that the
transcript of a previous trial should be treated differently than any other
statement. As well, the record discloses that the cross-examination was not
abusive in any way. Therefore, with respect, the trial judge was in error to
prevent any cross-examination unless there was a serious discrepancy arising in
the witness's testimony.

[
57
]

However, the error was of no importance. The
accused attempted, and succeeded, in getting the witness to admit that his
notes were an interpretation of what the accused had taught as opposed to a
direct statement of the accused. The accused's comments at trial indicated that
is what he wanted to do with the transcript, and he accomplished this without
having to cross-examine directly on the transcript. Further, this was not a
situation where the accused desired to impeach the credibility of the witness,
and required the direct reference to the original trial transcript for that
purpose.

[
58
]

The second complaint deals with the
cross-examination of Trudi Roth. The accused asked this witness if she was
familiar with two different documents which were not in evidence, and with
certain facts contained in those documents. The Crown objected to the accused
making those statements of alleged fact when posing questions to the witness.
The court was not concerned with the accused's manner of questioning. However,
the trial judge granted an adjournment to allow the Crown to substantiate its
objection. The court then directed the accused to simply ask the question
whether or not the witness was familiar with a document. If the answer was
"yes", then the accused was told he could ask the witness what she
knew about the document.

[
59
]

In my opinion, there was nothing improper in the
way the trial judge handled the Crown's objection. The accused was not
foreclosed from cross-examining the witness with respect to the documents.
Rather, the accused had to first inquire whether the witness was aware of the
document before proceeding. If the answer was no, the accused was directed to
not pursue questions regarding the content of those documents.

[
60
]

This is the proper approach when cross-examining
expert witnesses. In
R. v. Marguard
(1993),
1993 CanLII 37 (SCC)
, 85 C.C.C. (3d) 193 (S.C.C.)
at 230, McLachlin, J., writing for the majority, stated:

The proper procedure to be followed in
examining an expert witness on other expert opinions found in papers or books
is to ask the witness if she knows the work. If the answer is "no",
or if the witness denies the work's authority, then that is the end of the
matter. Counsel cannot read from the work, since that would be to introduce it
as evidence. If the answer is "yes", and the witness acknowledges the
work's authority, then the witness has confirmed it by the witness' own
testimony. Parts of it may be read to the witness, and to the extent they are
confirmed, they become evidence in the case.

This is a sensible approach to take when posing
questions to lay witnesses as well. Of course, lay witnesses cannot attest to
the authority of the facts or opinions expressed in the documents. Such a
witness may only testify that he is aware of the existence of the document and
to what extent he knows its contents.

a.

that questions cannot be put to a witness when
based on material which is not in the evidence, or where the facts behind the
question cannot be directly proved. There is authority that such questions are
within the discretion of counsel with the proviso that the answer given by the
witness to such questions stand: see R. v. Bencardino and De Carlo (1973),
1973 CanLII 804 (ON CA)
, 15
C.C.C. (2d) 342 (Ont. C.A.).

[
61

In sum, there was no error in the way the trial
judge dealt with the Crown's objection to the way the accused was
cross-examining Roth.
