suggest you might, because of giving of the response, put too much emphasis on
it or it might get you off on a tangent we didn't want you to get on, because
the charge itself that I gave you I've been working on for a long time, and I
gave it to you as carefully as I could without suggesting to you or ever having
you think that you should go one way or the other. [A.B. 4263-64]

[
78
]

Counsel for the appellant submits that the trial
judge did not adequately deal with the jury's request to have a copy of the
transcript of Mr. David. In particular, he argues that the transcript of an
important witness should have been given where it was readily available. He
also complains that the trial judge erred in failing to provide the jury with a
copy of the relevant
Criminal Code
sections or, alternatively, to
provide further explanation of those sections. The jury questions are said to
evidence a substantial lack of understanding and that the law requires such
questions be answered. In addition, the Appellant's counsel argues that the
issue was decided on the unrepresented accused's uncertainty.

[
79
]

The Crown responded that it is
"presumptuous" to assert that the jury's questions indicated a
substantial lack of understanding. As well, the Crown contended that the
unrepresented accused was quite reluctant for the jury to have a transcript of
Mr. David's testimony and was not uncertain as contended by the Appellant's
counsel. Further, the Crown submits that the trial judge's explanation for not
giving the transcript, namely that he did not want the jury to put too much
emphasis on that witness's evidence, and the additional comment that the jury
should not let that witness make the decision for them, were comments that hurt
the Crown's case and were effectively beneficial to the accused. As such, the
Crown submits that the Appellant cannot complain about an aspect of the trial
which was favourable to them.

[
80
]

On the question of supplying
Code
sections
to the jury, the Crown submits that it is a matter of discretion for the trial
judge, and that the concern in not giving provisions to the juries is that they
may place there own interpretations on the sections and not raise these types
of questions with the trial judge. As well, the Crown submits that an accurate
explanation of the sections which would have accompanied handing the sections
to the jury would not have improved the accused's position. Therefore, even if
an error was thought to have occurred in relation to supplying the jury with a
copy of the
Code
sections, the Crown submits that this would not have
improved the Appellant's position and that s. 686(1)(b)(iii) should be applied
to uphold the guilty verdict.

[
81
]

The adequacy of the trial judge's response to
the jury's requests is the pivotal issue of this appeal. As such, it demands a
thorough review of the applicable case law. The law regarding giving
transcripts or reviewing evidence with a jury, and the propriety of providing
the jury with
Criminal Code

sections will be treated separately. It must
be noted, however, that there is some overlap of the principles on these
issues.

A.
Request for the Transcript

[
82
]

For a starting point, the Supreme Court has
provided some general guidance on how jury questions ought to be dealt with. In
R. v. W.(D.) (1991),
1991 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, 63 C.C.C. (3d) 397 (S.C.C.), Cory, J. referred to some
general guidelines in responding to such questions at 410-11:

When a jury submits a question, it gives
clear indication of the problem the jury is having with a case. Those questions
merit a full, careful and correct response. As well, the answer should remind
the jury of its instructions given in the course of the main charge: see R. v. Desveaux
(1986),
1986 CanLII 153 (ON CA)
, 26 C.C.C. (3d) 88 at p. 93, 51 C.R. (3d) 173, 13 O.A.C. 1 (Ont. C.A.), where it was said:

Questions from a jury manifest
their concern and indicate their desire for direction on a particular issue.
The trial judge should read the question to counsel and obtain their
submissions as to the response that should be made. It is incumbent then on the
trial judge to answer the question in a complete and reasonably detailed
manner. It is unfair to the parties and the jury to attempt a short form answer
to a problem that is obviously presenting difficulties. The definitions
requested had been adequately set out early in the charge. However, memories
are short and much had intervened in the way of directions and recharges before
the question was submitted. The original instructions should have been repeated
in the response.

[
83
]

The Supreme Court referred to the issue of
satisfying a jury request for transcripts in R. v. Ostrowski.
1990 CanLII 116 (SCC)
, [1990] 2 S.C.R.
82. In this case, Cory, J. delivered the judgment of the court holding that the
trial judge did not err in refusing to provide the jury with the requested
transcripts. Here, the jury requested the transcripts of all of the witnesses,
and seven witnesses in particular. The request was received soon after the
completion of the trial in circumstances where it was speculative that
deliberations had begun or that the jury had formulated a specific reason for
the request. Cory, J. emphasized that the trial judge did not foreclose or
discourage the jury from making further requests for assistance stating (at
83):

Further the trial judge was careful not
to close the door to this request. He suggested that they begin their
deliberations based on their collective recollection of the evidence. However,
he specifically invited the jury to come back if after they had commenced their
deliberations they needed further assistance in this regard. He indicated that
at that time he would read from his notes pertaining to the witnesses or if
necessary obtain the transcripts. No objection to this response was taken by
the experienced counsel appearing for the appellant. No further request was
made by the jury for the transcripts. The jury deliberated until shortly in the
afternoon the following day at which time they delivered their verdict. In
those circumstances, it cannot be said that any error was made by the trial
judge.

[
84
]

The Supreme Court of Canada has issued two other
decisions on related points. First, it was held that it is an error for the
trial judge to only read back a portion of the direct examination and not read
the qualifying evidence or cross-examination when satisfying a jury request to
rehear portions of evidence: R. v. Olbey (1979),
1979 CanLII 61 (SCC)
, 30 N.R. 152 (S.C.C.).

[
85
]

And in
Cathro
v.
The Queen
(1955),

1955 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, 113 C.C.C. 225 (S.C.C.), the court took a cautious approach to giving
transcript portions or
Code
sections to a jury to aid them in their
deliberations. In this case, the trial judge furnished the jury with a copy of
the section of his charge that dealt with the applicable law. The court held
that (at 240):

It may be that a section of the Code, or
even a small passage of a learned trial Judge's charge, with the consent of
counsel concerned, may be handed to the jury, but even then the question must
remain whether, in the circumstances, there has been prejudice or miscarriage
of justice. Where, however, as here, the transcribed part of the charge
contains important references to the evidence and contentions made on behalf of
the Crown, and but slight reference to the evidence and none to the contentions
on behalf of the defence, there can be no doubt but that the giving of such
portion to the jury ought not be permitted.

[
86
]

This court addressed the issue of fulfilling
jury requests for transcripts in R. v.
Dorset
(1980),
1980 ABCA 246 (CanLII)
, 54 C.C.C. (2d) 490 (Alta C.A.). The central issue in
Dorset

was whether the trial judge erred in refusing to grant the jury's request for
transcripts of four Crown witnesses, and whether this resulted in a substantial
miscarriage of justice. Writing for the court, I held the following (at
493-94):

In my view, the jury in the case at bar
was entitled to be assisted in its deliberations. The learned trial Judge could
have informed the jury of the difficulties inherent in preparing transcripts at
the particular time, but he was obliged to provide the information requested,
even by reading his notes if necessary: see
R.
v.
Andrews
,
supra.

Considering that three of the requested transcripts were already available and
the fourth was less than 15 pages in length, the refusal of the jury's
reasonable request amounts to an error in law.

The evidence which was requested by the jury was
on the critical issue of identification, and I found that the refusal of the
trial judge to provide the jury with the transcripts or a reasonable
alternative resulted in prejudice to the appellant and miscarriage of justice.

[
87
]

In
Dorset
, I relied in part on
R.
v.
Wydryk and Wilkie
(1971),

1971 CanLII 1206 (BC CA)
, 5 C.C.C. (2d) 473 (B.C.C.A.). In that case, the jury returned after
deliberating for some hours and requested that the evidence of several key
identification witnesses be read back. The trial judge told the jury that they
would have to review the entirety of the evidence which would take
approximately 14 hours. He then requested that the jury retire and consider if
they wanted to hear all of the evidence. The jury returned and informed that
they were unable to reach a unanimous verdict. The trial judge then reminded
the jurors of their duty and urged them to reach a verdict. The accused were
subsequently found guilty. In holding that the trial judge erred in his
response to the jury's request, Bull, J.A. held (at 479) that:

Although I do not for a moment doubt that
a trial Judge when faced with a request by a jury to have certain evidence read
to them, may properly tell the jury the time that would be involved and any
other pertinent matters which he thinks should be brought to their attention
with respect to the request, I am of the opinion that in this particular case
the learned trial Judge erred in law with respect to the basis upon which he
asked them to reconsider their request.

Bull, J.A. concluded at 480:

In result, the trial Judge, through an
unfortunate misunderstanding of the applicable rule of law, unwittingly misled
the jury and effectively discouraged them from insisting on having that which
they required and which they were entitled. In my opinion, the appellant Wilkie
was prejudiced and there has been a miscarriage of justice.

[
88
]

There are two other British Columbia Court of
Appeal cases on this issue. In
R.
v.
Thomas
(1987),
1987 CanLII 2528 (BC CA)
, 20 B.C.L.R.
(2d) 241 (C.A.), the accused
was charged with second degree murder. During the course of the trial, a
psychiatrist gave important evidence relating both to intent and the insanity
defence. The importance of this testimony was highlighted by the fact that
portions of the precise words used by the psychiatrist were reviewed by both
defence and Crown counsel in their jury addresses and by the trial judge in his
charge. After deliberating for approximately six hours the jury returned with a
request for a copy of the relevant
Criminal Code

sections and for a
transcript of the evidence of the psychiatrist.

[
89
]

In response to these requests, the trial judge
read the
Code
sections, but he told the jury that they would not receive
the transcript for fear that they might place undue emphasis on that testimony.
Both counsel were satisfied with this response. Lambert, J.A., writing for the
court, held that the trial judge should have given what reasonable assistance
he could in responding to the requests subject to not jeopardizing a fair
trial. Mr. Justice Lambert was also amenable to providing the jury with the
requested transcript. Drawing on the concurring judgment of Goodman, J.A. in
the Ontario Court of Appeal decision in
R.
v.
Corriveau
,
infra,

he said at 250:

I would extend Mr. Justice Goodman's
analogy by asking whether it is reasonable for a judge, sitting alone, to call
for a transcript of part of the evidence if he wishes to study the exact words.
Surely it is. Indeed, it may be essential. And if it is reasonable or essential
for a judge to obtain a transcript in those circumstances, then, subject to
appropriate safeguards, it might well be reasonable or even essential for a
transcript of the same part of the evidence to be given to the jury.

[
90
]

Noting that the psychiatrist's precise words
were of crucial importance, it was held to be error for the trial judge not to
provide the jury with a transcript. Lambert, J.A. held that the trial judge
should have at least inquired whether the jury wanted to examine whether the
precise words, or whether a reading of the evidence would have been sufficient.
In either case, it was held that the trial judge should have asked what precise
segments of the evidence were required, and having found that out, the jury
should have been supplied with whatever they reasonably required.

[
91
]

Lambert, J.A. also commented on the role of
counsel with respect to jury requests. He stated at 252:

I do not think that the fact that no
objection was taken by defence counsel, at the time, to the course which the
trial judge adopted has the effect of curing what would otherwise be a
miscarriage of justice: see
Stirland
v. D
.P.P.
,
[1944] A.C. 315
at 328, 30 Cr. App. R. 40, [1944] 2 All E.R. 13 (H.L)
, and
R.
v.
Stewart
,

supra.
There may be cases where a failure to object will prevent an
error from being treated as a miscarriage of justice. But this is not one of
them. It is not the role of defence counsel to waive the jury's rights. His
role does not extend beyond his own client's rights.

[
92
]

The failure of the trial judge to adequately
respond to the jury's requests was held to have resulted in a miscarriage of
justice demanding a new trial.

[
93
]

Most recently, the British Columbia Court of
Appeal dealt with a similar issue where the jury requested certain
psychological reports in
R.
v.
De Bellefeuille
, (24 January 1994)
Vancouver 130/CA016341. The trial judge denied this request on the basis that
these reports were not put in evidence and further told them "you will
have to manage on the evidence that your do have". Following this, after
further deliberating for just over an hour, guilty verdicts were returned.
Prowse, J.A., writing for the court, held that the trial judge's response was
inadequate as there was no inquiry as to the nature of the jury's concern, and
that the answer may have had the effect of discouraging the jury from seeking
further assistance. She held that given the importance of the evidence to the
defence, there was a miscarriage of justice demanding a new trial.

[
94
]

The Ontario Court of Appeal has also had several
opportunities to comment on the issue of providing the jury with requested
transcripts. First, in
R.
v.
Andrade
(1985),
1985 CanLII 3502 (ON CA)
, 6 O.A.C. 345, the
jury returned after deliberating for only fifty minutes requesting the
transcript of the entire proceedings. Martin J.A., writing for the court, noted
that it is well established that the jury is entitled to have the court reporter
read back the evidence of a witness. However, on the facts of this case, he
distinguished the prior cases of
Wydryk and Wilkie
,
supra,
and
Dorset
,

supra,
stating at 366:

In my view, the response of the trial
judge in the present case to the jury's request, made soon after they had
retired to consider their verdict, that it was not possible to provide them
with a transcript of the entire evidence, did not contravene the principles
enunciated in those cases.

Although Martin J.A. felt it would have been
preferable for the jury to be reminded at that time that the evidence could be
read back or reviewed in the judge's notes if clarification was needed, the
jury was previously made aware of this entitlement. Consequently, the Court of
Appeal held that there was no reversible error.

[
95
]

In
R.
v.
Corriveau
(1985),
1985 CanLII 3550 (ON CA)
, 8
O.A.C. 18 (Ont. C.A.), the jury
came back after two hours' deliberation to request the transcripts of four
witnesses. No transcripts were available at the time, but counsel were informed
that a typed summary of the judge's notes could be provided. The Crown agreed
with this suggestion, but defence counsel insisted on the reporter reading back
the entirety of the evidence arguing that the jury wanted the exact wording.
The Crown then suggested that the jury be asked if there were any specific
portions of the evidence which they were concerned about. However, the judge
rejected this suggestion being of the opinion that all of the evidence would
have to be read.

[
96
]

In holding that the trial judge erred in law in
his handling of the jury's request which required a new trial, MacKinnon
A.C.J.O., in the majority judgment, made the following comments at 22:

In my view, he should have offered to
review his notes of the evidence with regard to these four witnesses for the
jury. He is responsible for his charge and the instructions and the fact that
counsel for the accused may have taken an unreasonable position does not
relieve him from his responsibility.

Alternatively, as suggested by Crown
counsel, he should have asked them if there were specific areas of the lengthy
evidence that they wished to hear. He did neither and, in my view, he was in
error in not assisting the jury in the way or ways mentioned.

In effect, by directing the jury to
"retire and continue your deliberations", the jury could conclude
that he was rejecting their request simpliciter. That error was an error in law
and fatal to the conviction.

[
97
]

In addition, as noted in
R.
v.
Thomas
,

supra,
Goodman J.A. in a concurring judgment, was of the opinion that a
jury, as the sole finder of fact, is entitled to the same assistance a judge
sitting alone would have, and is entitled to the benefit of the notes of the
official court reporter if it is unsatisfied as to the completeness or accuracy
of their collective memory of the evidence.

[
98
]

The final Ontario case dealing directly on this point is
R.
v.
Callaghan

(1991),
1991 CanLII 7234 (ON CA)
, 5 O.R. (3d) 508 (C.A.).
The jury in
Callaghan
, after deliberating for several hours, requested
the transcript of the complainant's testimony. They were informed that a
transcript was not available and that it would take about two hours to read
back the evidence. The foreman of the jury offered to tell the judge in general
terms what they were looking for, but the trial judge told them that this would
not be appropriate as it would disclose the jury's concern. As well, the trial
judge informed the jury of the danger that they might overlook something when
seeking the passages they were concerned about if the entire evidence was not
read to them. The jury retired to further deliberate and returned an hour later
with a guilty verdict.

[
99
]

Drawing on
R.
v.
Andrade
,
supra,

the court noted that it is not incumbent that a jury hear the entire
evidence of a witness when they are requesting only certain portions of the
testimony, only that the trial judge must ensure that all of the evidence
pertaining to a particular area be included. In this regard, Krever J.A. for
the court said at 511:

It is possible that that part of the
evidence that the jury was concerned about was so closely related to so much of
the remaining evidence that it would be difficult to segregate a discrete
portion or discrete portions of the testimony. The trial judge's refusal to
permit the foreman to describe the jury's concern makes it impossible to know
whether that was the situation in this case. I am unable to say that the jury's
verdict would inevitably have been the same had the proper procedure been
followed and, accordingly, it is my view that the conviction cannot stand.

A new trial was consequently ordered.

[
100
]

The final case is the recent Manitoba Court of
Appeal decision in
R.
v.
Foti
,
1993 CanLII 14722 (MB CA)
, [1994] 1 W.W.R. 385. In this case,
approximately one and a half hours after deliberations began, the jury
requested a transcript of the key identification witness. Twaddle J.A., writing
the main judgment, endorsed the view of British Columbia Court of Appeal in
R.

v.
Wong
(1978),
1978 CanLII 2367 (BC CA)
, 41 C.C.C. (2d) 196, where McFarlane J.A. said at 204:

There has been some diversity of opinion
among Canadian Courts about the propriety of giving juries written extracts
from evidence or from a Judge's charge, memoranda of law, or copies of relevant
sections of a statute. The predominant view appears to disapprove. I do not
think absolute condemnation is justified. On the other hand, it is no doubt a
dangerous procedure and should, I think, be adopted only in very special
circumstances and with great care.

Drawing on these comments, Mr. Justice Twaddle
disapproved of a general principle that a juries should routinely be supplied
with transcripts. He was of the opinion that such a requirement would be
impractical and counterproductive to the due administration of justice as
transcripts would rarely be transcribed in time for the jury's deliberations.

[
101
]

The court in
Foti
was at first inclined
to find that the trial judge had a discretion to deny the jury's request,
particularly in light of the virtually faultless jury charge and what the court
viewed as a lack of obligation to provide a jury with transcripts. However,
Twaddle J.A.'s assessment of the applicable case law led him to decide that the
court is obligated to give some assistance to the jury. He said at 395:

It thus seems clear that a trial judge
has a duty to assist a jury in their recollection of the facts when requested.
The form of assistance which he offers them is a matter, I think, within the
discretion of the judge, but he cannot withhold his assistance because of the
difficulties of giving it. Nor can he rely on the literal truth of a statement
that the transcripts are not available. He must offer the jury some assistance,
enquire of them what point is troubling them (and respond to it) or, at least,
leave the door open for them to return if their collective memory proves
insufficient.

[
102
]

Since the requested evidence was crucial to the
case, s. 686(1)(b)(iii) was held to be inapplicable and a new trial was
ordered.

Summary of Principles

[
103
]

Several principles with regard to supplying the
jury with requested evidence arise from these authorities. First, since it is
clear that questions or requests from juries normally indicate that they are
experiencing difficulty in their deliberations, such questions, as Cory J.
pointed out in
R.
v.
W.(D.)
,
supra,
must be given a
"full, careful, and correct response."

[
104
]

Second, in order to avoid jeopardizing the
fairness of the trial, the trial judge must be careful when responding to jury
requests. In most instances, this would be accomplished by simply ensuring that
the jury receive any pertinent or qualifying evidence when providing a review
of the requested testimony.

[
105
]

Third, a trial judge must not simply deny a
jury's request for evidence or other assistance. A judge presiding over a jury
trial has an absolute duty, except in very limited circumstances, to provide a
jury with some form of assistance when a question or request indicates that
they are experiencing difficulty.

[
106
]

Fourth, the most appropriate method of
assistance would, in my opinion, depend on the circumstances of the case. In
this regard, I note Mr. Justice Twaddle's concern in
R.
v.
Foti
,
supra,

that the administration of justice must not be impeded by a general
requirement that transcripts be supplied to juries when the transcripts are not
readily available. However, unlike the court in
Foti
, I do not voice any
general disapproval of such a practice. The preferable view was taken in
R.

v.
Thomas
,
supra,
where the particular facts of a case may make
it reasonable, if not essential, that the jury be able to study the exact words
used by a witness. In addition, I agree in principle with Goodman J.A. in
R.

v.
Corriveau
,
supra,
that since a judge sitting alone would have
recourse to the court reporter's notes if needed, so should the jury. However,
I recognize that particular circumstances may create an exception, and that a
review of the trial judge's notes or a read back of the evidence by the court
reporter may be sufficient.

[
107
]

Fifth, the trial judge's obligation to provide
assistance to jury does not depend on the consent of counsel. Although there is
reference in
Cathro
,
supra,
that
Code
sections or small
passages of a Judge's charge may be given handed to the jury "with the
consent of counsel," I do not read this case to create a requirement that
the consent of counsel must be obtained in every instance before a jury is
supplied with transcripts or other assistance. This is not to say that the
submissions of counsel are unimportant. Indeed, the proper procedure is to seek
the positions of counsel before supplying responding to jury questions (
R.

v.
W.(D.)
,
supra
). This procedure protects the fairness of a
trial. Similarly, the failure of experienced defence counsel to object to a
trial judge's course of actions in some circumstances may be a relevant
consideration in determining whether a miscarriage of justice has occurred.
However, as noted in
R.
v.
Thomas
,
supra,
it is not the
prerogative of defence counsel, or the Crown for that matter, to waive the
jury's right to assistance. As noted in
R.
v.
Corriveau
.

supra,

the fact that counsel may have taken an unreasonable position does not
relieve the trial judge of his or her responsibility to render assistance to
the jury.

[
108
]

Sixth, if the jury's request is interpreted as
being too broad, the trial judge must then ascertain what the core of their
difficulty really is and, having done so, then determine what they reasonably
need to resolve it. The only requirement is that the trial judge protect the
fairness of the trial by ensuring that the jury receive all of a witness's
evidence touching on a particular issue.

[
109
]

Finally, the jury must not be discouraged from
seeking further assistance, rather they should be encouraged to do so. When
responding to jury questions which may be interpreted as too wide, it is
incumbent of the trial judge to remind the jury that they are entitled to the
court's assistance on any point of evidence on which their collective
recollection is unclear. They may be informed of any difficulties in satisfying
a request, but this must not be done in a way which would discourage them from
seeking further help.

Analysis

[
110
]

In my opinion, the trial judge, with respect,
committed reversible error in responding to the jury's request for the
transcript of Dr. David. Simply denying to supply the jury with the requested
evidence in some form was an abrogation of the trial judge's duty to provide assistance
to the jury. The trial judge should not have decided this issue on the lack of
consent of either the accused or Crown counsel. The jury's right to assistance,
and the trial judge's duty to provide the jury with that help, transcends any
position counsel may take. Additionally, this was not a situation where the
jury was requesting the transcripts on the speculative basis that it may aid
them. The jury had already deliberated for several hours. Their request for the
transcript and the
Code
sections leaves no question that help was
needed.

[
111
]

In this situation, the request for the
transcript of Dr. David's evidence articulated that help was needed, and it was
error on the part of the learned trial judge to simply refuse to provide the
transcript. Particularly as this evidence was most important from the
standpoint of the Crown and the defence. The Crown submitted that David's
evidence established that the accused's teachings were outside the social
studies curriculum. The accused argued the opposite saying that the curriculum
guide called for conflicting ideologies and that there was no proof that his
classes went beyond the guide. The trial judge indicated the significance of
David's evidence by inviting them to compare his evidence to the curriculum
guide and with the evidence of two of the students. As well, Dr. David's
evidence was stated to be relevant to the s. 319(3)(c) defence. The trial judge
suggested to the jury that if they found the accused's teachings were within
the allowed curriculum, it would be significant evidence that it was for the
public benefit. Conversely, he suggested that if the subjects taught were not
within the curriculum, that would be some evidence of the discussion not
falling under the realm of public benefit.

[
112
]

Knowing that the requested evidence was
important to the case, it was a serious error to deal with the jury's questions
in such a cursory manner. As Lambert, J.A. said in
R.
v.
Thomas
,
supra,

at 251:

At the very least, the trial judge ought
to have found out whether the jury wanted to examine the precise words at their
leisure, or whether a reading of the evidence would be sufficient, and, in
either case, he ought to have tried to identify the precise segments of the
evidence that were required, and then, having found that out, he ought to have
provided whatever the jury reasonable required.

That duty could not be discharged by merely
suggesting that the jury subsequently could lead more specific questions.
Indeed, the reasons given by the learned trial judge for the reluctance to give
them the transcript, i.e. that too much emphasis might be placed on it, would
discourage the jury from asking specific questions about it or making any
further requests in connection with it. Had the transcripts been what was
required, it must be noted that they were immediately available and the jury's
deliberations would not have been disrupted in fulfilling that request.

B.
Request for the Criminal Code Provisions

[
113
]

In order to assess whether the trial judge erred
in not providing the jury with copies of the
Criminal Code

sections, it
is first necessary to examine the propriety of doing so. There is some
divergence of opinion on this point.

[
114
]

This court took a permissive stance in
R.

v.
Read
(1984),
1984 ABCA 161 (CanLII)
, 31 Alta. L.R. (2d) 364. The appropriateness of giving
the jury copies of the relevant
Code
sections was referred to at 370-71:

If there is value in reading these
sections to the jury, the value would lie in their remembering what was read.
But clearly they cannot remember the wording of a section and it seems only
sensible to us that they be given copies of the section quoted to them so that
when they weigh the judge's explanation about the sections that he had read,
they will at least have the sections about which he had been speaking before
them.

[
115
]

The only other reported decision from Alberta on this issue is
R.
v.
Matt

(1967),
1967 CanLII 742 (AB SCTD)
, 60 W.W.R. 571 (Alta. S.C.). In this case, Riley, J. clearly indicated that it was not
inappropriate to provide the jury with unannotated
Code
sections if the
jury makes the request in open court. He stated at 573:

It seems to me that any jury is entitled
to refresh its memory as to the exact terms of the law, and while the jury must
accept the law as laid down by the trial judge, it sometimes happens that the
jury are the better informed, and more sure, if it has the printed word to
reinforce the spoken -- the spoken perhaps not being fully remembered in exact
terms.

[
116
]

A similar position was taken by the Quebec Court
of Appeal in
R.
v.
Stanford
(1975),
1975 CanLII 1335 (QC CA)
, 27 C.C.C. (2d) 520. Berier,
J.A. held, at 526, that where the trial judge takes the trouble of reading the
text of
Criminal Code

sections to the jury,

it is not only permissible but even
prudent to give them the text rather than let them use their memory, the
reliability of which is questionable in such a foreign area.

[
117
]

In
R.
v.
Siu
(1992),
1992 CanLII 1014 (BC CA)
, 71 C.C.C. 197
(B.C.C.A.), the court was of the opinion that the jury should be given
Criminal
Code

sections in difficult cases, but that it would be preferable for the
jury to receive the extracts prior to the jury charge.

[
118
]

The Saskatchewan Court of Appeal, in
R.
v.
Schimanowsky
(1973),
1973 CanLII 919 (SK CA)
, 15
C.C.C. (2d) 82 and
R.
v.
Crothers
(1978),
1978 CanLII 2527 (SK CA)
, 43 C.C.C. (2d) 27, has
taken an opposite position. In those cases, the court condemned the practice of
giving juries
Criminal Code

sections. The stated rationale for this
position was that even if the sections were given to a jury to aid them in
understanding a judge's instructions on the law, the danger of the jury placing
their own interpretation on the law would outweigh any benefit. The court
viewed the jury seeking further instructions from the trial judge as the proper
approach.

[
119
]

More moderate stances have been taken in a
number of other decisions. These cases have generally disapproved of the
practice of giving the jury
Criminal Code

extracts, but have held that
it is not a reversible error to do so when the jury is given accompanying
instructions on the law and cautioned not to engage in their own
interpretation: see
R.
v.
Wong
,
supra;

R.
v.
Flewwelling

(1984),
1984 CanLII 5572 (NS CA)
, 63 N.S.R. (2d) 382 (N.S.C.A.);
R.
v.
Vawrvk and Applevard

(1979),
1979 CanLII 3079 (MB CA)
, 46 C.C.C. (2d) 290 (Man. C.A.);
R.
v.
Decloedt and Widenmaier

(1986),
1986 CanLII 4671 (MB CA)
, 28 C.C.C. (3d) 7 (Man. C.A.).

[
120
]

The Ontario Court of Appeal has taken the
position that, while juries should not be encouraged to seek copies of
statutes, it is entirely within the trial judge's discretion to give
Code
sections
to the jury as long as the jury is cautioned not to engage in independent
interpretations of the provisions. This position was stated in
R.
v.
Tennant
and Naccarato
(1975),
1975 CanLII 605 (ON CA)
, 23 C.C.C. (2d) 80 at 102:

There are many cases in which the charge
must contain instructions as to a number of sections of the
Criminal Code
.

In such cases it might be helpful to the jury to have copies of the sections as
an aid to recalling accurately the numerous elements of the sections to which
they had been referred by the trial Judge in his charge. Accordingly, we are
not prepared to say that a trial Judge must not provide copies of sections of
the
Criminal Code
to a jury. Each case will depend upon its own
circumstances. The more complicated the issues the more likely the jury is to
request copies of the sections of the
Code
to assist them; and the more
likely is the trial Judge to decide that copies of the relevant sections of the

Code
may assist the jury in their difficult task.

This view was affirmed in the later case of
R.

v.
Tuckey
(1985),
1985 CanLII 3509 (ON CA)
, 46 C.R. (3d) 97 (Ont. C.A.), where it was held to be within the trial judge's discretion to
provide the jury with
Code
extracts even without a request from the
jury.

[
121
]

These authorities, on the whole, establish that
not only is it permissible for a trial judge to provide copies of the
Code
to
the jury, it may be judicious to do so. As stated in
R.
v.
Read
,
supra,

and
R.
v.
Stanford
,
supra,
it is sensible and even
prudent to give the jury copies of the
Code
where the sections have been
read to the jury by the trial judge. Other cases have indicated that having the

Code
sections read to the jury is not necessarily a prerequisite to the
jury receiving them. There may be cases where the complexity of the relevant
legal provisions would make it advisable for the jury to receive the text of
those sections.

Analysis

[
122
]

Several factors in the present case establish
that it would not only have been permissible but even prudent for the trial
judge to provide copies of the
Code
sections to the jury. First of all,
the trial judge read and reread both the offence and defence provisions to the
jury as well as reading the
Criminal Code

definitions for
"communicating" and "statements".

[
123
]

Second, the relevant
Code
sections are
complex. The offence provision in
s. 319(2)
alone contains several elements
which were given full explanations by the trial judge. Similarly, the statutory
defences, all of which contain several distinct components, required extensive
instructions.

[
124
]

Third, additional difficulties were inherent in
the s. 319(3)(a) truth defence. Because this defence contains a reverse onus,
the trial judge was required to pay special attention to distinguishing the
balance of probability onus on the accused for that defence as opposed to the
onus remaining on the Crown to negative the other statutory defences.

[
125
]

Finally, the trial judge underscored the
complexity of the relevant provisions by repeatedly referring to the provisions
and their component parts throughout a lengthy portion of his charge.

[
126
]

In sum, it is not surprising that the jury
returned with a request to view or rehear provisions. The provisions are
complex with each containing several elements. It is clear that the jury would
have been aided by having the relevant sections before them.

[
127
]

Despite the fact that the jury would have been
aided by having the
Code
sections, it is not a requirement that they
receive them. The Crown is correct in asserting that this is a matter within
the trial judge's discretion. Accordingly, no reversible error can be
attributed to the judge in not fulfilling the jury's request for the
Code
sections
themselves. Indeed, the jury asked to either see or hear the provisions, they
were not necessarily demanding copies. However, the trial judge should have at
least reread the provisions or have given additional instruction on the law.
The failure to do so is a reversible error as the jury request indicated that
they were in need of additional help with regard to the relevant
Code
provisions.

C.
Section 686(1)(b)(iii)

[
128
]

The next step is consider whether these errors
can be dealt with by s. 686(1)(b)(iii) of the
Code.
Section
686(1)(b)(iii) provides that an appeal may be dismissed:

(iii) notwithstanding that the court is
of the opinion that on any ground mentioned in subparagraph (a)(ii) the appeal
might be decided in favour of the appellant, it is of the opinion that no
substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice has occurred;

[
129
]

In deciding this issue, it is noted that the
cited cases which deal with providing a review of evidence or transcripts to a
jury indicate that the failure to adequately assist the jury in its
deliberations usually results in a new trial. It was only those cases such as
R.

v.
Andrade
,
supra,
and
R.
v.
Ostrowski
,
supra,
where
it was clear that the jury had not yet encountered a specific difficulty that a
miscarriage of justice did not occur.

[
130
]

In addition, I note that the present case is
somewhat similar to
R.
v.
Bordonaro

(1986), 20 O.A.C. 339
. In
that case, the trial judge inadvertently failed to address a question submitted
by the jury. This was held to be a grave error which was incapable of being
cured by s. 686(1)(b)(iii) [then s. 613(1)(b)(iii)]. Although the trial judge
did not completely fail to address the jury's questions in the present case, it
was similarly a substantial error to decline the jury's requests and give them
no assistance whatsoever.

[
131
]

In my opinion, it is not possible to apply s.
686(1)(b)(iii) in this instance. The evidence of Dr. David was stated to be
both important to the Crown's case and to the defence. It is impossible to
discern, as the Crown suggests, that the comments made by the trial judge in
response to the jury's requests for Dr. David's evidence were beneficial to the
accused. As well, the
Criminal Code

sections were complex and the
request for the provisions indicated that the jury needed help. Similarly, the
Crown submission that an accurate description of the law would not have aided
the accused cannot be assessed. It is therefore impossible to find that no
substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice occurred in the case at bar. I
would allow the appeal and quash the conviction. It must then be considered
whether a new trial should be ordered.

Ordering a New Trial

[
132
]

Under s. 686(2) of the
Code,
this court
has the discretion to order a new trial or to direct a verdict of acquittal
where the trial judge has made a wrong decision on a question of law. The
ultimate issue in this appeal is whether the accused should face a third trial.
Several cases have referred to the exercise of this discretion.

[
133
]

In
Dunloo and Sylvester
v.
The Queen

(1979).
1979 CanLII 20 (SCC)
, 47 C.C.C. (2d) 93 (S.C.C.), two accused were directly implicated in a
rape, but were also charged as parties. The majority of the Supreme Court held
that the trial judge erred in charging the jury that the accused could be
convicted as parties to the offence as their was no evidence to substantiate
that allegation. This error was held to be incurable by s. 613(1)(b)(iii) since
it was impossible to determine what basis the jury convicted on. In determining
that it was a proper case in which to direct a verdict of acquittal, Dickson,
J. (as he then was) stated (at p. 113):

For the following reasons given by Mr.
Justice Hall, I would direct a verdict of acquittal, rather than have the
applicants undergo a third trial [at p. 98]:

The accused have been subjected to two
trials and a like number of appeals. They have been in custody over a year. The
doubt raised on their innocence or guilt should be resolved by now. The
substance of the case is their denial against the testimony of Ross, without
much more. In the circumstances, the needs of justice would be met by directing
a verdict of acquittal, rather than having the accused submit to a trial for
the third time.

[
134
]

In
R.
v.
Sophonow (No. 2)
(1986),
45 C.C.C. (3d) 415 (Man. C.A.), the accused was charged with murder, and the
case was dependent on dubious identification evidence. The court was unanimous
in holding that a new trial should not be held stating (at 461):

In the short reasons delivered at the
time our judgment was pronounced, my brother O'Sullivan, speaking for the
court, said:

In considering this question we
are satisfied that we ought to take into account the fact that the accused has
already been tried three times and has served three years and nine months in
custody without bail. The Supreme Court of Canada in Dunlop and Sylvester v. The Queen … expressly held that those
are proper considerations for us to take into account in coming to a decision.

…

I am also of the view that the quality of
the identification evidence would not be improved by its further repetition, as
that would only give the witnesses an opportunity of being even surer than
before. Finally, I am concerned that it would be difficult, in view of the
notoriety the case has gained, to which I made a reference at the beginning of
these reasons, to find a jury of 12 citizens totally uninfluenced by what they
have seen or heard already.

[
135
]

In
R.
v.
Haslam
(1990),
1990 CanLII 166 (BC CA)
, 78 C.R.
(3d) 23 (B.C.C.A.), the trial judge was held to be in error in failing to put
the defence of non-insane automatism to the jury. The accused in this case was
charged with the aggravated assault of her husband. The majority of the court
decided that a new trial should not be ordered. Counsel for the accused cited
several reasons why an acquittal should be directed. These included that it
would be the third trial, the accused had been subjected to restrictive bail
terms during the two years the proceedings had occupied, the accused had served
nine day's imprisonment out of a 60 day sentence at the second trial, and she
was a good candidate for early release. Aside from these submissions, the
majority of the court placed special importance on the trial judge's finding of
fact that the accused's husband had subjected her to numerous acts of violence
and that she displayed the "battered wife" syndrome.

[
136
]

This court's power under s. 686(2) to direct a
verdict of acquittal is purely discretionary and does not have to meet the
stringent standard for ordering an abuse of process set out in
R.
v.
Jewitt

(1985),
1985 CanLII 47 (SCC)
, 47 C.R. (3d) 193 (S.C.C.). However, the principles followed and factual
contexts in which the abuse of process doctrine arises are of assistance.

[
137
]

In
R.
v.
Conway
(1989),
1989 CanLII 66 (SCC)
, 49 C.C.C. (3d) 289 (S.C.C.), L'Heureux-Dube, J., writing
for the majority, commented on the abuse of process doctrine (at p. 302):

It acknowledges that courts must have the
respect and support of the community in order that the administration of
criminal justice may properly fulfil its function. Consequently, where the
affront to fair play and decency is disproportionate to the societal interest
in the effective prosecution of criminal cases, then the administration of
justice is best served by staying the proceedings.

[
138
]

Keyowski
v.
R.

(1988),
1988 CanLII 74 (SCC)
, 62 C.R. (3d) 349 (S.C.C.) held that multiple trials may constitute an
abuse of process without any prosecutorial misconduct, but that three trials in
itself is not an abuse of process. In
Keyowski
, the accused was charged
with criminal negligence causing death. Several factors were cited in the
decision to refuse a stay: a serious charge was involved, the three years and
seven months taken in the proceedings was not undue, and the accused had not
been held in pre-trial custody. Although the court recognized that the accused
had suffered significant trauma and stigma from the proceedings and the
attendant publicity, that was seen to apply to the vast majority of accused.
Overall, the administration of justice was seen to be best served by allowing a
third trial.

[
139
]

In
R.
v.
Mitchelson
(1992),
1992 CanLII 4018 (MB CA)
, 13
C.R. (4th) 73 (Man. C.A.), the court ordered a stay of proceedings in a summary
conviction proceeding for an alcohol-related driving offence. The accused in
this case was a prominent member of the Winnipeg city council. In deciding whether a fourth trial should be held,
the court accepted the submission that the accused is entitled to the same
considerations any person in similar circumstances would have. The court cited
several factors in the decision to stay the proceedings. First, three years
time over which the time had occupied was seen as undue. Second, no previous
cases could be found where an accused was subjected to a fourth trial for a
single summary conviction charge. Finally, the publicity generated by the accused's
charge due to his prominence in the community evidenced that he had been both
stigmatized and punished, and had been held accountable in another forum.

[
140
]

Several factors militate in favour of a new
trial. First of all, the accused was not subject to any detention during the
ongoing proceedings, nor was he subject to any restrictive bail conditions.
Secondly, the accused's ability to get a fair trial would not be any different
if a third proceeding was ordered. Potential juror's may still be challenged
for cause, and it may even be easier to empanel impartial jurors if public
interest in this case wanes. Third, the quality of the evidence would not
change appreciably for a new trial. The second trial proceeded on past
recollection recorded evidence for all but two of the former students. This
documentary evidence is still available and its quality will not be any
different at a third trial.

[
141
]

Two factors are somewhat neutral. First, it is
unknown what effect these proceedings have had on the accused. Trauma and
stigma are certainly involved in the proceedings, but as Wilson, J. noted in
R.
v.
Kevowski
,

supra,
this is true for the vast majority of accused.

[
142
]

A second neutral factor is the amount of time
these proceedings have occupied. It has been nearly 10 years since the
indictment was originally laid. Certainly the accused has attributed to this
extraordinary amount of time by appealing his convictions. However, the Crown
also contributed by appealing to the Supreme Court of Canada. Blame for this
amount of time should not be levelled on either side. The justice system was
dealing with a little used
Criminal Code

section which demanded
constitutional assessment. I therefore view the 10 years to date not as undue, but
as an inherent problem faced in dealing with the applicable
Code
provisions.

[
143
]

There remains the question of whether any
additional time and resources should be expended on this indictment. The answer
lies in the societal interest pursuing a third trial. As L'Heureux-Dube, J.
stated in
R.

v.
Conway
,
supra,
the functioning of the courts depends on the respect
of the community in the administration of criminal justice.

[
144
]

I question whether public respect for the
criminal justice system would be enhanced by a third four-month trial. A new
trial would provide at public expense yet another opportunity for the Appellant
to propound his views at length. It would expose the witnesses (who in the main
have no independent recollection of the facts) and the community to a third
ordeal of a four-month trial in a decade. Whatever the results, it can only
serve to exacerbate the harm and injury already done to both the target group
and society in general. The administration of justice would be best served by
bringing the case to an end.

[
145
]

Since drafting these reasons, I have had the
opportunity of perusing the judgments of my brother Foisy, J.A. and my sister
Hetherington, J.A. In order to avoid an unseemly impasse in the disposition of
this appeal, I would dispose of it in the manner set out by my Lady
Hetherington. I am sure that the Attorney-General will carefully weigh all of
the implications involved in the conduct of a third trial..

DATED at Calgary,

Alberta this 7th day of
September,

1994.

REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT OF

THE HONOURABLE MADAM JUSTICE HETHERINGTON

[
146
]

I have read the reasons for judgment of Mr.
Justice Harradence and Mr. Justice Foisy. I agree with Mr. Justice Harradence
that the trial judge erred in responding to questions from the jury. And I
agree with him that for this reason, the conviction must be set aside. I would
not, however, substitute for it an acquittal. I would order a new trial.

[
147
]

The jury sent a note to the judge which he read
in open court as follows (AB 4252):

"Could we get Mr. David's transcript,
and for clarification could we hear or see the
Criminal Code
of the
charge."

After discussing it with counsel for the Crown
and Mr. Keegstra, the trial judge responded to the note at some length. Much of
the response dealt with matters not connected with the questions from the jury.
In relation to those questions, the trial judge said that he was not going to
answer them. He asked the jury to be more specific if they required assistance.
In particular he said (AB 4261-4265):

"… we have the questions that you've
asked, and we've had a full discussion, the end result of which is it is our
view that we should not give you or should not respond to those questions in
the form in which you have framed them. So I say that as time wears on if you
have more specific questions, I want to invite you to write them out and send
them out, as I indicated was your right.

….

… and there is some authority in the
courts to suggest that we should deal, perhaps, with more specific questions
rather than something in general, but in particular, not to give -- if we can
do it some other way -- a transcript of a witness's evidence.

Now, the
second issue that you raised, which I assume from the note was the charging
section of the
Criminal Code
that gave rise to the charge in the Indictment
that Mr. Keegstra faces; it's one in which I gave the same response to you on.
And again, I ask the same of you, that if there is something specific or more
specific than what you asked, then I want you to tell us. We have an obligation
to give you assistance, but we have an obligation also not to do -- not to give
you assistance where someone might suggest you might, because of giving of the
response, put too much emphasis on it or it might get you off on a tangent we
didn't want you to get on,….

….

So in the end,
the decision has been made here that we should not give you that for which you
ask but that we want you to come back with anything that you feel you want some
further help with; and we'll evaluate it and determine whether we can or we cant
and the manner in which we can give it to you….."

[
148
]

The difficulty with this response is that the
questions contained in the note from the jury were very specific. I do not know
how the jury could have made them more so.

[
149
]

The problem with the jury's request for a
transcript of the evidence of Dr. David was not that the request was not
specific. The problem, as the trial judge saw it, was that Mr. Keegstra and
counsel for the Crown were not in agreement as to what assistance he should
give to the jury in relation to this request. Mr. Keegstra did not think that
he should give them the transcript, and counsel for the Crown did not think
that he should read them his notes. As a result, the trial judge simply refused
to comply with the request of the jury.

[
150
]

I agree with Mr. Justice Harradence that a trial
judge's obligation to provide assistance to a jury does not depend oh the
consent of counsel or the parties. A transcript of the evidence of Dr. David
was available. That evidence was very extensive. In the Appeal Book, it covers
300 pages. The trial judge might well have been reluctant to give the jury such
a lengthy transcript. If so, he should have communicated his concern to the
jury, and asked whether they really needed a transcript of all of the evidence,
or whether they could identify particular parts which they required. He could
also have inquired as to whether he could asist them by reading them his notes,
or whether they wanted the exact words of the witness. However, he should have
made it clear to them that he would comply, one way or another, with their
request for assistance with the evidence of Dr. David. No one suggested to him
or to us that this request was unreasonable.

[
151
]

Unfortunately, the trial judge did not do any of
these things. He simply told the jury to ask more specific questions if they
needed help, without telling them how they could do so. This response might
well have discouraged the jury from asking further questions.

[
152
]

The trial judge understood the jury's question
in relation to the
Criminal Code
to be a request for "the charging section
and perhaps the defences as set forth in the Code." It seems to me that
this is clearly what they wanted, and that the question was quite specific.
Again counsel for the Crown and Mr. Keegstra disagreed as to whether the trial
judge should comply with this request. Mr. Keegstra thought that he should.
Counsel for the Crown thought that he should not.

[
153
]

The charging section was s. 319, the relevant
parts of which read as follows:

"319.(1) ….

(2) Every one who, by communicating
statements, other than in private conversation, wilfully promotes hatred
against any identifiable group is guilty of

(a) an indictable offence ….

(3) No person shall be convicted of an
offence under subsection (2)

(a) if he establishes that the
statements communicated were true;

(b) if, in good faith, he
expressed or attempted to establish by argument an opinion upon a religious
subject;

(c) if the statements were
relevant to any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the
public benefit, and if on reasonable grounds he believed them to be true; or

(d) if, in good faith, he intended
to point out, for the purpose of removal, matters producing or tending to
produce feelings of hatred towards an identifiable group in Canada."

[
154
]

In his charge to the jury the trial judge read
and explained each of the subsections quoted above in turn. The jury asked him
to read these subsections again. Because counsel for the Crown would not agree,
he refused. Again he told them to ask more specific questions if they wanted
help, without telling them what he meant. The jury did not ask any more
questions. In the end result, therefore, the jury asked for assistance with the
law, and did not get it.

[
155
]

It is not necessary in this case to decide whether
the trial judge should have given the jury a copy of the parts of
s. 319
quoted
above. He read them in giving his charge to the jury. He should at least have
read them again, when the jury asked him to do so. If necessary, he could have
given the jury further instructions, or cautioned them to remember his previous
instructions, about these subsections.

[
156
]

For these reasons, in my view the conviction
cannot stand. I would set it aside. I would not, however, substitute for it an
acquittal.

[
157
]

Mr. Justice Harradence has carefully analyzed
the factors which militate for and against a new trial in this case. I can add
nothing to this analysis. He concluded that the administration of justice would
best be served by bringing this case to an end. While I find his reasoning
attractive, I do not agree that it would be apropriate for this Court to bring
the case to an end. I would allow the appeal, quash the conviction and order a
new trial.

this 7th day Of September,
