REASONS FOR
JUDGMENT OF

THE HONOURABLE MR. JUSTICE FOISY

[
158
]

The appellant was tried by judge and jury and
convicted of the following offence:

"That he, between the 1st day of
September, A.D. 1978, and the 31st day of December, A.D. 1992, inclusive, at or
near the Town of Eckville, in the Province of Alberta, did wilfully promote
hatred against an identifiable group, to wit: the Jewish people, by
communicating statements while teaching students at Eckville High School,
contrary to the provisions of the
Criminal Code
.
"

[
159
]

Section 319(2)
and
(3)
of the
Criminal
Code
,
R.S.C. 1985, c. 46
read as follows:

"(2) Every one who, by communicating
statements, other than in private conversation, wilfully promotes hatred
against any identifiable group is guilty of

(a) an indictable offence and is liable
to imprisonment for a term not exceeding two years; or

(b) an offence punishable on summary
conviction.

(3) No person shall be convicted of an
offence under subsection (2)

(a) if he establishes that the statements
communicated were true;

(b) if, in good faith, he expressed or
attempted to establish by argument an opinion upon a religious subject;

(c) if the statements were relevant to
any subject of public interest, the discussion of which was for the public
benefit, and if on reasonable grounds he believed them to be true; or

(d) if, in good faith, he intended to
point out, for the purpose of removal, matters producing or tending to produce
feelings of hatred towards an identifiable group in Canada."

[
160
]

Some 15 grounds of appeal were advanced by the appellant
during the course of the hearing. After hearing the appellant on all 15
grounds, 11 of these were dismissed from the bench and the Crown was called
upon to respond to four grounds of appeal. These are as follows:

"Issue 1A: Are Words such as 'public
interest', public benefit', 'religious subject', 'race', 'religion', 'ethnic
origin', and 'hate' void for vagueness under section 7 of the
Charter?

Issue 1B: Did the trial judge err in his
definition of public interest and public benefit assuming these words are not
so vague as to be constitutionally invalid?

Issue 4: The trial Judge erred in unduly
restricting the cross-examination and set bad precedent rulings in the way of
an unrepresented accused who is properly cross-examining the instances of Maddox
(Vol. 2, p. 397, line 20 and
p.
412,); Roth (p. 562); Ramstead (p. 953)
from their evidence in a previous trial.

Issue 10: The Trial Judge erred in not
giving the jury (a) a copy of the transcript of Robert David's evidence when
requested and (b) a copy of the
sections 319(2)
and
(3)
of the
Criminal Code
on
request."

[
161
]

I have had the advantage of reading the reasons
for judgment given by ray brother Harradence, J.A., and I agree in the result
with respect to the first three issues. I only wish to add a few comments and I
will deal with them in the order in which Harradence J.A. has discussed them.

[
162
]

The first issue is the constitutional issue,
namely, whether words such as "public interest" and "public
benefit", as they appear in s. 319(3)(c), are void for vagueness under s.
7 of the
Charter.

I would note that the Supreme Court of
Canada in
R. v. Keegstra (No. 1)

(1990),
1990 CanLII 24 (SCC)
, 61 C.C.C. (3d) 1
(S.C.C.) has already decided that
s. 319(2)
and
(3)
are saved by s. 1 of the
Charter

in the context of any violation of s. 2(b) and s. 11(d)
Charter

rights. In my view, any violation in the context of a
Charter

s. 1 debate, as it relates to
s. 319(2)
and
(3)
, would meet with the same
result.

[
163
]

Vagueness, as a separate constitutional point
under s. 7 of the
Charter,
only arises where the law is so
lacking in precision as to be unable to give sufficient guidance for a legal
debate: see
R. v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society

(1992),

1992 CanLII 72 (SCC)
, 93 D.L.R. (4th) 36 (S.C.C.). This court, in
R. v. Keegstra

(No. 2)
(1991),
1991 ABCA 97 (CanLII)
, 63 C.C.C. (3d) 110, has already addressed this point at p.
122 by saying:

"Another
ground invokes s. 11
(g)
of the Charter, which protects an accused from
condemnation under
ex post facto
laws. The provision in the
Code
under
review was, of course, in force during the charge period. His argument is that
it had not, in all respects, been interpreted by the courts, and therefore the
accused did not know the law against him. This is akin to a void-for-vagueness
argument: see
R. v. Stagnitta
(1987),
1987 ABCA 153 (CanLII)
, 36 C.C.C. (3d) 105,43
D.L.R. (4th) 111, 54 Alta. L.R. (2d) 1 at p. 12 (C.A.). It is not clear at all that such a rule exists in Canada under the aegis of s. 7. If it does,
it should resemble the 'prescribed by law' test for s. 1. That test, in turn,
demands that the legislation be 'intelligible': see
Irwin Toy Ltd. v.
Quebec
(Attorney General)

(1989),
1989 CanLII 87 (SCC)
, 58 D.L.R. (4th) 577, [1989] 1
S.C.R. 927, 94 N.R. 167 at p. 229. That test is met here. The dispute among
courts about the constitutional validity of this law should not be
misunderstood. No great dispute existed about its meaning. The provisions in
question are capable of interpretation. This ground fails."

[
164
]

The appellant's criticism of the use of the word
"hatred" has already been settled by the Supreme Court in
R. v.
Keegstra (No. 1)

as indicated above. I agree with Harradence
J.A.'s conclusion with respect to the use of the words "religion",
"religious subject", "race", and "ethnic origin".
Like him, I am of the view that the appellant's submission with respect to the
use of these words is void of any merit.

[
165
]

With respect to the words "public
interest" and "public benefit", it is difficult to understand
how the court would strike down provisions of the
Criminal Code

that form part of defences available to the accused on the ground that they
are vague due to overbreadth. Firstly, as stated by the Supreme Court in
R.
v. Nova Scotia Pharmaceutical Society
,
overbreadth does not exist
independently. At p. 306 Gonthier J. says:

"I would therefore conclude that:

1. What is referred to as 'overbreadth',
whether it stems from the vagueness of a law or from another source, remains no
more than an analytical tool to establish a violation of a Charter right. Overbreadth
has no independent existence. References to a 'doctrine of overbreadth' are
superfluous."

[
166
]

Secondly, it is even more difficult to
understand how the appellant could successfully attack words from part of the
defences available to him on the grounds that they are vague due to overbreadth.
What possible prejudice could there be upon the "life, liberty, and
security of the person" if the criticism is that Parliament has provided
too large a scope for the defences to a
s. 319(2)
offence?

[
167
]

The appellant relies on the Supreme Court of
Canada's recent decision in
R. v. Morales

(1992),
1992 CanLII 53 (SCC)
, 77
C.C.C. (3d) 91 (S.C.C.) as authority for the proposition that the words
"public interest" offend the
Charter

for
vagueness. It should be noted that in
Morales

s. 11(e) of
the
Charter

was engaged in the context of pretrial
incarceration and the presumption of innocence. It was in that context that the
Supreme Court had difficulty in finding a working meaning for the words
"public interest". Considerations relating to the presumption of
innocence and pretrial custody can hardly be said to apply to prosecutions
under
s. 319(2)
of the
Criminal Code
.

[
168
]

That point was made by the Ontario Court of
Appeal in
R. v. Farinacci et al,
(8 November 1993) Nos. C10791, C13886 and
C11372, and B.C. Court of Appeal in
R. v. Branco
(8 November
1993) No. 015818, where both courts declined to apply
Morales

when
dealing with the term "public interest" as it is used in
s. 679(3)
(c)
of the
Criminal Code

(dealing with postconviction
release). I consider the words of Finch J. A. in
Branco

at
p. 10 to be applicable to this case where he says:

"The appellant's liberty interest
can only be enhanced by s. 679(3)(c), under which the operation of the sentence
imposed by the trial judge may be temporarily suspended."

Similarly here, the use of the impugned
provisions would seem to enhance the appellant's defence rather than deprive
him of any rights that he has under s. 7 of the
Charter.

[
169
]

Lastly, the appellant relies on the decision of McLachlin
J. in
R. v. Zundel
(No. 2)
(1992),
1992 CanLII 75 (SCC)
, 140 N.R. 1 (S.C.C.). In that
case, her Ladyship concluded that the words "injury or mischief to a
public interest" found in
s. 181
of the
Criminal Code

could
not be saved under s. 1 of the
Charter.

Unlike the court's
finding in
Keegstra (No. 1
),
those words in the context of s. 181
of the
Criminal Code

did not meet the proportionality test
which was found to have been met when considering
s. 319(2)
and
(3)
of the
Criminal
Code

in
Keegstra (No. 1).
It was her view that in
contrast to the pressing problem in
Keegstra (No. 1),
(that is
the dissemination of hate propaganda, particularly racial hate propaganda), no
such social problem was in issue with respect to s. 181 of the
Criminal
Code.

That McLachlin J.'s criticism of the words "mischief
to any public interest" is related to the legislation's objective is
evident by her remarks at p. 38:

"…It is difficult to see how a
broad, undefined phrase such as 'public interest' can on its face constitute a
restrained, appropriately limited measure which impairs the right infringed to
the minimum degree consistent with securing the legislation's objectives…"

[
170
]

The answer to the appellant's argument is simply
that in
Keegstra (No. 1)

the Supreme Court concluded that,
bearing in mind Parliament's objectives in enacting
s. 319(2)
and
(3)
, the
proportionality test had been met and that the legislation was neither vague
nor overly broad. The same legislative objectives are absent in considering
s.
181
of the
Criminal Code

in the context of s. 1 of the
Charter.

[
171
]

The second issue to be considered is the
criticism of the trial judge's definition of the words "public interest"
and "public benefit" as they appear in
s. 319(3)
(c) of the
Criminal
Code
.

If the trial judge's definition of these words to the jury
in his charge was vague, then the appellant's challenge to the charge is even
more so. It becomes difficult to answer the appellant's complaints in the
absence of any specificity. In any event, in reaching its verdict, it was clear
that the jury had concluded that this appellant had wilfully promoted hatred
against the Jewish people, that the truth of the statements had not been
established, that he had not expressed or attempted to establish an opinion on
a religious subject in good faith, that he had no reasonable grounds to believe
the statements to be true, nor that he in good faith intended to point out for
the purpose of removal, matters producing or tending to produce feelings of
hatred towards the Jewish people. Keeping these findings in mind, along with
the plethora of accusations made against the Jewish people, it is inconceivable
that the "public interest" or the "public benefit" could
ever be engaged in the circumstances of this case.

[
172
]

The third ground of appeal in Mr. Justice Harradence's
reasons for judgment deals with restrictions on cross-examination of certain
witnesses during the trial. My reading of the materials makes it abundantly
clear that the trial judge was attempting to assist the appellant at every
turn. I can do no better than agree with Harradence J.A.'s comments that any
error made by the trial judge in this context would have been minimal at best
and did not result in any prejudice to this appellant.

[
173
]

With respect to the fourth issue, I respectfully
disagree with Harradence J.A.'s conclusions. For the following reasons I
conclude that the procedure employed by the trial judge, in the circumstances
of this case, does not amount to reversible error and accordingly I would
dismiss the appeal. I should add that Harradence J.A's reasons contain a
thorough review of the relevant case law. I do not intend to repeat these cases
except to emphasize certain areas which I consider to be pertinent. I would
also add that in my view the case law simply exemplifies the common sense rule
that a trial judge has a duty to assist the jury in a reasonable fashion. The
trial judge has to be given some leeway regarding how this will be
accomplished. In the end cases will be decided on an individual basis having
regard to the situation in each case.

[
174
]

After deliberating less than four hours, perhaps
as little as three hours, allowing time for the evening meal, the jury requested
"Mr. David's transcript, and for clarification could we hear or see the
Criminal
Code

of the charge". The transcript requested by the jury
was some 300 pages in length, and both the appellant and Crown counsel objected
to the trial judge simply giving the jury the transcript requested. While the
trial judge ultimately has to make the decision, the positions taken by counsel
and the appellant are relevant considerations to be taken into account by the
trial judge. See
R. v. Cathra,
1955 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1956] 113 C.C.C. 225 (S.C.C.),
R.
v. Grover

(1990),
1990 CanLII 11030 (ON CA)
, 56 C.C.C. (3d) 532 (Ont. C.A.) (appeal allowed and new trial ordered
by Supreme Court of Canada for other reasons).

[
175
]

In
Cathro

Estey J. said at
p. 240:

"It may
be that a section of the Code, or even a small passage of a learned trial
Judge's charge, with the consent of counsel concerned, may be handed to the
jury, but even then the question must remain whether, in the circumstances,
there has been prejudice or miscarriage of justice…"

[
176
]

Also in
Grover

Tarnopolsky
J.A., in deciding that a certain response given by the trial judge to the jury
was not an error, said the following at p. 536:

"It is
important to recall that the learned trial judge was strongly urged by defence
counsel to give the response he did and that Crown counsel, after some
hesitation, acceded to that advice…"

[
177
]

Also in
R. v. W.
(D.)

(1991),

1991 CanLII 93 (SCC)
, 63 C.C.C. (3d) 397 (S.C.C.) at 410-11, Cory J. quoted from the Ontario Court of
Appeal in
R. v. Desveaux

(1986),
1986 CanLII 153 (ON CA)
, 26 C.C.C. (3d)
88

at
93, 51 C.R. (3d) 173, 13 O.A.C. 1:

"…Questions from a jury manifest
their concern and indicate their desire for direction on a particular issue.
The trial judge should read the question to counsel and obtain their
submissions as to the response that should be made. It is then incumbent on the
trial judge to answer the question in a complete and reasonably detailed
manner. It is unfair to the parties and the jury to attempt a short form answer
to a problem that is obviously presenting difficulties. The definitions
requested had been adequately set out early in the charge. However, memories
are short and much had intervened in the way of directions and recharges before
the question was submitted. The original instructions should have been repeated
in the response."

[
178
]

Accordingly, valid positions taken by counsel
should be considered by the trial judge in deciding how best to discharge his
or her duty vis-à-vis the jury. This the trial judge did here.

[
179
]

With respect to the jury's request for the
transcript of Mr. David's evidence, this is what the trial judge told the jury:

"…the end result of which is it is
our view that we should not give you or
should not respond to those
questions in the form in which you have framed them.
So I say that as time
wears on
if you have more specific questions, I want to invite you to write
them out and send them out, as I indicated was your right.

The concern, I
suppose, is that when one wants some specific thing that one side or the other
feels might bear unfavourably on the positions they take, there's usually
always a reason why there's a reluctance to give it, and I think there's a
general uncomfortable feeling in giving something in a general way -- for
example, the entire transcript of a witness's evidence -- because of the fear
that too much emphasis might be placed on it over the other evidence; which of
course brings me to the re-call yesterday and to comments made during the trial
itself by Crown counsel, by Mr. Keegstra, and perhaps by me -- and by me in the
summation or in the directives that I gave you yesterday -- which is twofold to
say to you on re-call, or as it is with receiving answers to questions, to not
put more emphasis on that than what you put on the directions that you were
given by me in general."

[Emphasis Added]

[AB Vol. 23, p. 4262]

"And
that, of course, may be part of the reason there is some reluctance on our part
-- and there is some authority in the courts to suggest
that we should deal,
perhaps, with more specific questions rather than something in general, but in
particular, not to give -- if we can do it some other way -- a transcript of a
witness's evidence."

[Emphasis Added]

[AB Vol 23, p. 4263]

[
180
]

It should be noted that Mr. David's evidence was
particularly damaging to the. appellant's defence. The appellant forcefully and
correctly made the point to the trial judge that there was a danger to him in
simply putting the 300 pages of transcript before the jury without more. In the
circumstances, and in view of the appellant's valid objection, the course taken
by the trial judge was not unreasonable.

[
181
]

As I said before, there is a duty upon the trial
judge to assist the jury in any reasonable way. For example, this court held in

R. v. Dorset

(1980),
1980 ABCA 246 (CanLII)
, 54 C.C.C. (2d) 490 (Alta. C.A.), that an outright refusal by the
trial judge to provide transcripts or to assist the jury in any other manner
amounted to reversible error.

[
182
]

However, the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Ostrowski
,
1990 CanLII 116 (SCC)
, [1990]
2 S.C.R. 82, Cory J. held at p. 83:

"…The jury asked for a transcript of
all the witnesses and particularly of seven named witnesses, five of whom gave
evidence relating to Ostrowski. It would be speculative to say that the jury
had even commenced their deliberations by this time or had formed a precise
reason for the request.

Further, the trial judge was careful
not to close the door to this request. He suggested that they begin their
deliberations based on their collective recollection of the evidence. However,
he specifically invited the jury to come back if after they had commenced their
deliberations they needed further assistance in this regard.
He indicated that at that time he would read from his notes
pertaining to the witnesses or if necessary obtain the transcripts. No
objection to this response was taken by the experienced counsel appearing for
the appellant. No further request was made by the jury for the transcripts. The
jury deliberated until shortly in the afternoon the following day at which time
they delivered their verdict. In those circumstances, it cannot be said that
any error was made by the trial judge." [Emphasis Added]

[
183
]

Also in
R. v. Thomas

(1987),

1987 CanLII 2528 (BC CA)
, 20 B.C.L.R. (2d) 241 (C.A.) the
court decided that trial judge's refusal to provide a transcript requested by
the jury amounted to reversible error. However, Lambert J.A., speaking for the
court at p. 251, said:

"…
At the very least, the trial
judge ought to have found out whether the jury wanted to examine the precise
words at their leisure, or whether a reading of the evidence would be
sufficient, and, in either case, he ought to have tried to identify the precise
segments of the evidence that were required, and then, having found that out,
he ought to have provided whatever the jury reasonably required, subject only
to whatever safeguards were necessary, if any, in order to ensure a fair trial.
"

[Emphasis added]

[
184
]

In a recent decision of the Manitoba Court of
Appeal,
R v. Foti

(1993),
1993 CanLII 14722 (MB CA)
, [1994] 1 W.W.R. 385, the court
was critical of routinely giving the jury transcripts of evidence or other
written material. Twaddle J.A. endorsed the view of the British Columbia Court
of Appeal in
R. v. Wong

(1978),
1978 CanLII 2367 (BC CA)
, 41 C.C.C. (2d) 196, where
McFarland J.A. at 204 said:

"…it is no doubt a dangerous
procedure and should, I think, be adopted only in very special circumstances
and with great care…"

[
185
]

Twaddle J.A. then went on to say at p. 395

"It thus seems clear that a trial
judge has a duty to assist a jury in their recollection of the facts when
requested. The form of assistance which he offers them is a matter, I think,
within the discretion of the judge, but he cannot withhold his assistance
because of the difficulties of giving it. Nor can be rely on the literal truth
of a statement that the transcripts are not available.
He must offer the
jury some assistance, enquire of them what point is troubling them (and respond
to it) or, at least, leave the door open for them to return if their collective
memory proves insufficient."

[Emphasis
Added]

[
186
]

A number of cases were cited to us on this issue
with the result differing depending on whether or not in the circumstances of
each case the trial judge's obligation to the jury had been reasonably
discharged.

[
187
]

In this case the trial judge did not refuse to
assist the jury. Quite to the contrary he invited the jurors to focus in on
whatever particular problem or problems they were having and to return to him
for assistance. This was a reasonable alternative to simply giving the jury 300
pages of transcript, particularly when jury deliberations had been in progress
for only a short time and the appellant and Crown counsel objected to this
option with some degree of validity.

[
188
]

The same comment can be made with respect to the
trial judge's response to the request made by the jury "for clarification
could we hear or see the
Criminal Code

of the
charge".

[
189
]

The trial judge responded to this request as
follows:

"Now, the
second issue that you raised, which I assume from the note was the charging
section of the
Criminal Code

that gave rise to the charge in the
Indictment that Mr. Keegstra faces; it's one in which I gave the same response
to you on. And again, I ask the same of you, that if there is something
specific or more specific than what you asked, then I want you to tell us. We
have an obligation to give you assistance,…"

[AB Vol. 23,
pp. 4263-64]

"So in
the end, the decision has been made here that we should not give you that for
which you ask but that we want you to come back with anything that you feel you
want some further help with; and we'll evaluate it and determine whether we can
or we can't and the manner in which we can give it to you…"

[AB Vol. 23,
p. 4265]

[
190
]

The question posed by the jury was somewhat
vague, and again the trial judge did not refuse to assist the jury but simply
asked them to be more specific and that he would endeavour to assist them.

[
191
]

It should be noted that the trial judge had given
the jury a lengthy and detailed explanation with respect to
s. 319(2)
as well
as all of the defences under
s. 319(3)
of the
Criminal Code
.

That
the trial judge has a discretion to exercise in deciding whether to give the
jury sections of the
Criminal Code

is not in dispute. In
the exercise of that discretion the court must take care not to prejudice the
outcome of the trial. In this case, giving the jury sections of the
Criminal
Code

or rereading them to the jury would have probably involved
a complete and lengthy recharge on all of the issues relating to ss. 319(2) and
(3) of the
Code.

While it may have been necessary
ultimately to do so, it was not unreasonable for the trial judge to ask the
jury to attempt to be more specific, and to seek his assistance if needed,
particularly when he had just given the jury a full explanation of the law a
few short hours previously.

[
192
]

The fact that the jury did not return with any
further questions is not an indication that they were discouraged from doing so
by the trial judge's answer. In my view, it is simply an indication that the
jury, after focusing on any specific problem or problems that they may have
had, as invited to do so by the trial judge, were able to resolve the problems
without returning to him for further assistance. That they had a right to
return for assistance was made very clear to them.

[
193
]

The decision of this court in
R. v. Read

(1984),

1984 ABCA 161 (CanLII)
, 53 A.R. 243 (C.A.) is cited in support of the appellant's submissions on this
point. In
Read

the trial judge had provided the jury with
copies of the sections of the
Criminal Code
.

The question
was whether or not this constituted reversible error. This court held that
provided adequate warning was given to the jury of the use they might make of
this material, there was no resultant error.

[
194
]

This is

not to say that the trial judge
is bound to provide sections of the
Criminal Code

to the
jury when requested. The trial judge may do so with adequate instructions as to
how the jury may use parts of the
Code.

In my view,
however, the trial judge is not bound to do so provided that the trial judge
otherwise adequately discharges his or her duty to assist the jury. Again,
here, the trial judge's request to the jury that they attempt to focus in on a
more specific problem or problems and that he would attempt to assist them, as
he was obliged to do, was not error.

[
195
]

Accordingly, I would dismiss the appeal.
